subtopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL FISCAL ARRANGEMENTS AND ESTABLISHED PROGRAMS FINANCING ACT, 1977 MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in speaking previously to this Bill, I was arguing that the Government should be expanding funding for post-secondary education rather than reducing the amount of funds that are available. I have also argued that these reductions in the amount of money that the federal Government is prepared to spend on post-secondary education will have a more serious effect, I believe, on both deaf and hard of hearing Canadians. At the present time access to higher education is limited for deaf and hard of hearing students. There is a lack of program services and facilities. Among other problems, there are insufficient note-takers, interpretative services, special preparatory programs, sound amplification systems and other facilities to give them equal access to post-secondary educational opportunities.
[DOT] (mo)
The need for greater access to advanced technical programs for the deaf and hard of hearing is critical. Modern technology and computer sciences will have an enormous impact on our society. Our hearing impaired population can stand to benefit greatly from extensive training. It is estimated that there are between 30 and 40 deaf students in Canadian universities.
Statistics are not available as to the enrolment of hard of hearing students in Canadian universities. The universities and colleges with hearing impaired students have attempted to provide some support services. Such services may take the form of notetakers or sign language interpreters but these services are not structured into an ongoing program.
In the past and until as recently as the fall of 1982, deaf students capable of progressing to a higher education had the limited options of attempting to compete with their hearing peers to gain access to a regular university or community college and then struggle through the program with or without support services, depending on the availability of such services.
Another option is to seek access to an existing institution which has initiated some form of support services or even the Gallaudet College entrance examination for acceptance into a program specifically designed to meet the needs of the hearing impaired. There are about 120 Canadian citizens currently attending Gallaudet College in the United States.
The third option is no longer available to deaf Canadians at the preparatory level because the rubella epidemic in the United States in 1963-64 created an unusually high number of college-age American deaf students seeking admission to Gallaudet College. It is worth while pointing out, as I did previously in this debate, Mr. Speaker, that there is absolutely no Canadian institution for deaf or hard of hearing students. If a deaf or hard of hearing Canadian wants to be educated or even gain access to post-secondary education, he or she has to go to the United States.
In addition to the problem of admittance, Canadian students are encountering other difficulties at Gallaudet College. Tuition fees have been increased and on-campus housing is limited. This has resulted in additional expenses for students as well as possibly increasing difficulties in finding suitable housing in the vicinity of the campus.
Given American statistics which show that 30 per cent of U.S. graduates of residential schools for the deaf will attend post-secondary institutions, it is expected that a similar percentage of Canadian deaf students would also want to pursue higher education. At this point it is crucial to indicate that even if the facilities of Gallaudet College are available to Canadian hearing impaired students, this College provides services only in English and is not accessible to deaf Francophones.
It is evident from the situation I have described that the time is long past when Canadians can safely rely on American institutions in order to educate their deaf youth at the university level. American Government-supported facilities must, by definition, give priority to their own citizens and should not be

April 10, 1984
Established Programs Financing
expected to compensate for the shortcomings of the educational system of another country, in this case Canada. Furthermore, it is highly questionable whether it is justifiable, both morally and financially, to deprive young people who will become the leaders of Canada's deaf community of a large part of their Canadian heritage by forcing them to be educated in a foreign country. To be effective Canadian leaders, they must be given the opportunity to grow in a Canadian environment, learning about Canadian society, politics, institutions and culture.
Hard of hearing students have special needs of their own which are usually not recognized unless specifically brought to the attention of the educational institutions. Usually these students are left to struggle through university or college with little or no support services. A hard of hearing student may need some simple and inexpensive sound amplification to supplement the personal hearing aid, the assistance of a note-taker or an overhead projector or some other appropriate device which could be provided if the facilities of universities and colleges were sensitized to the needs of hard of hearing students. Such sensitization will only come into being when formally structured, subsidized support services are made available as a matter of course.
More often than not a Canadian hard of hearing student would choose to continue to study in this country rather than in the United States-in this case in Washington-thus avoiding a move to another country and another culture. Gallaudet College is primarily intended for the deaf and the environment is rich in deaf culture.
This lack of opportunity about which I have spoken exists because post-secondary education of the deaf and hard of hearing has never been addressed on a national scale. Until the problem is addressed by way of a federally-funded study, then this problem will remain with us and will continue to squander a facet of one of our most important resources-Canadian hearing impaired youth.
In my view-and it is shared by my colleagues-the Government of Canada should fund a national study of postsecondary education of the deaf and hard of hearing. The national study group should include representatives from various organizations, institutions, as well as appropriate individuals. The purpose of the committee should be to focus on studying the development of multi-disciplinary facilities with emphasis on technical training, with full access to deaf and hard of hearing students. These facilities should encompass applied research and human resource development and should act as resource centres for the purpose of networking with other existing universities and colleges where there is an overlap of interest. I would hope that the recommendations of the proposed study committee would be supported by federal funding, which would then result in a solution of the difficulties confronting deaf and hard of hearing Canadians in their attempts to seek higher education.
The urgency of this matter cannot be over-emphasized. For too long the post-secondary educational needs of the deaf and hard of hearing have lacked attention. As 1985, the International Year of Youth, approaches, it is particularly timely that action be taken on this important issue. The Canadian Coordinating Council on Deafness presented a brief to the Minister of State responsible for the disabled on this very important issue of access to the hearing impaired and deaf in the country.
Provincial and federal governments have been cutting back on post-secondary education for young people, but not because of any lack of resources, as has been argued by the federal Government and provincial governments, in particular in my case the Government of Ontario.

There is absolutely no question about that, Mr. Speaker. Shortly after the last Parliament convened, I along with other Members of the House served on the Special Committee on the Disabled and the Handicapped. The Minister of State for Small Businesses and Tourism (Mr. Smith), by the way, was the Chairman of that particular committee. I would be remiss if I did not take this opportunity to mention that one of the hardest working members on that committee was the late Hon. Walter Dinsdale who had devoted much of his adult life to the concerns of the disabled in the country.

The testimony that we on that committee heard from witness after witness concerned access to education. Access to education for a person who happens to be disabled is extremely limited for a number of reasons. We cannot talk about access to education for someone who is disabled in isolation because it is so integral to the participation of the handicapped in the mainstream of Canadian life.
If we are not prepared to provide a disabled person with adequate access to education, then we are denying that disabled person the opportunity to find gainful employment, access to transportation, access to recreational facilities and access to all kinds of things that we able-bodied Canadians take for granted. That is why education is so crucial to a person who happens to be disabled. We must recognize that individuals such as blind Canadians who are attempting to gain access to the university education system or even to junior school require additional assistance that able-bodied Canadians do not need. Very often the family resources cannot provide for that and I would strongly argue, as our committee strongly argued, that the Government must play a role in allowing the handicapped and disabled to gain access to the various institutions in the country that we as able-bodied Canadians take for granted.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there is absolutely no question that that is so in a number of ways. First, the individuals I have encountered since I came to this place and since I was a member of that committee clearly indicated to me that the old stereotype of a disabled person being locked up in an institution and kept away from the mainstream of society no longer holds true at all. A person with disabilities is quite capable of being educated in the same way as anyone else. In fact, the stereotyping has got to the point where anyone with a disability has been considered to be somehow mentally deficient, and that is the worst kind of stereotyping I have ever encountered.
We should take a look at the straight economics of the situation, Mr. Speaker. Let me refer to figures based on estimates that are three or four years old; I am sure the figures are quite different today. However, if society continues to institutionalize individuals simply because of a disability or a handicap, it is not economical on a straight cost basis. It costs something like $35,000 and probably more like $40,000 or $50,000 a year to maintain a person in an institutional setting. If you provide them with the means to live within the community and with adequate community support services, the com-

April 10, 1984
Established Programs Financing parative cost is around $8,000 per year. Even on a straight economic basis it is much more effective for society to provide those individuals with the means to live within Canadian society as able-bodied Canadians, and to give them the opportunity to reach their own level in society.
Disabled Canadians have an expression for the able-bodied. They call them "tab" persons-that is, "temporarily able-bodied". Even while we enjoy good health and physical attributes, at some point in our life either through accident, illness or aging the possibilities of becoming disabled are extremely good.

subtopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL FISCAL ARRANGEMENTS AND ESTABLISHED PROGRAMS FINANCING ACT, 1977 MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am very pleased to have the opportunity to say a few words on Bill C-12. The first point I should like to make refers to statements made by the Hon. Minister when he moved second reading of the Bill on January 27. As reported at page 814 of Hansard he said:
-federal assistance to each province for post-secondary education will be increased by 6 per cent in 1983-84 and by an additional 5 per cent in 1984-85.
He emphasized the word "increased". A little later he said:
The purpose of this change is to clarify the fact that the federal Government contributes huge amounts to the provinces. Over $13.5 billion was contributed for 1983-84 to assist the provinces in financing post-secondary education and health programs.
The Hon. Minister continually used the word "increase", but when 1 look at the Bill I do not see anything in it about increases. As a matter of fact, on the first page of the Bill Clause 3 reads as follows:
"the fiscal equalization payment to each province for a fiscal year shall be reduced to the amount obtained-"
Not "increased", Mr. Speaker, but "reduced". On page 5a of the Bill a very tricky formula is set out under which the numerator is the per capita Gross National Product for the calendar year ending immediately preceding the calendar year ending in the fiscal year, and the denominator is the per capita Gross National Product of the fourth calendar year. It also refers to the cube root of the fraction, not the square root or result but the cube root. Anyone who knows anything about mathematics knows that the cube root is much smaller than the square root and much smaller than the actual result. This is another way of reducing the amount. As everybody knows, the cube root of 64 is 4 and the cube root of 27 is 3. The square root of 64 is 8. Here we have the cube root taken to find the amount of money going to the provinces.
An explanatory note to Clause 7 reads in part as follows:
-would provide for a 6 per cent limitation in the growth of the per capita entitlement applicable in respect of the education program to a province for the 1983-84 fiscal year and a 5 per cent limitation in the growth of that entitlement for the 1984-85 fiscal year.
Why did the Hon. Minister leave the impression with all those who heard his address but who have not had access to the Bill that the funds are going to be increased by the Bill? That is a pretty sneaky way of trying to fool the public. I do not think it is proper for a Minister to mislead the people.
Just recently a teacher said to me: "I heard we got an increase because I heard the Minister". I said: "How do you get an increase when you take the cube root of something?" She looked at me very oddly. I said: "Do you get an increase when you reduce the amount of money that is going to be paid to the provinces?" She said: "I do not know what you mean". I showed her the Bill and told her what has been happening. She said: "I was completely misled". When qualified teachers are misled, what about the general rank and file of the public? This is no way for the Government to act, Mr. Speaker. I deplore the method used by the Hon. Minister to make people think we are getting an increase when there is actually a decrease.
Let us examine the figures that are being applied. The Minister also applied the tax transfer agreement. That simply moved percentage points of the income tax from the federal Government to provincial governments. The same tax is applicable to the people of each province. Instead of the federal Government collecting the money the provincial government does so; then it is provincial money and not federal. Yet the Bill continually refers to the money being collected under a transfer agreement. If the federal Government wanted to use that figure as part of its contribution, then why did it transfer the percentage points in the first place? There is no reason for it, but once it has transferred the percentage points it becomes provincial money and the federal Government should not try to make people believe it is part and parcel of the program.
The Bill reduces the cash going to the provinces. Throughout the Minister's speech I do not think the word "reduction" was used once but the word "increase" was frequently used. That is very misleading.
The Bill applies different growth rates to education taxes for 1983-84 and limits the amount for 1983-84. In other words, it is retroactive legislation. This is 1984 and it is limiting the grants for 1983-84.
Another thing that I do not like about the Bill is that it is a unilateral change, not a change negotiated with the provinces but a change forced on the provinces whether they like it or not. That is not the way Canadians are used to doing business.
It seems to me that there is about $100 million that should be going to the provinces for education. But where is that money going? We have received no explanation from members of the Government. Where is the money going and what is it being used for? I think people are entitled to know that. As a member of this Party mentioned just the other day, the total tax grab is about $380 million. In 1983 it was $118 million and in 1984 $260 million. That money is being taken away from a proper allocation to the provinces.
When the Minister mentioned the 6 per cent and the 5 per cent that he is now going to use, in effect he is saying that the Government is going to chisel the provinces out of more than 2 per cent under the former Act. Actually the increase should be over 8 per cent instead of 6 per cent and 5 per cent. In other words, the Government is again chiselling the provinces out of money that the former Act gave to them.

Something which has become very commonplace throughout the years during which I have been watching the present Government in action is the encouragement given to the provinces to expand programs, to introduce new programs. Then when they introduce them, the federal Government withdraws its support and leaves them up to the provinces to continue. It has done this in many cases. This is a bad way for the Government of Canada to operate. If the federal Government wants to inject itself into the educational facilities, then once it does that, it should stay there and not continuously change its plans and programs unilaterally as it has been doing.
This Bill not only reduces the amount of money to the provinces but will actually lower the quality of education in this country. I realize that that is a serious charge and I make it only after reflecting on it carefully and studying the Bill. It cannot help but lower the quality of education in Canada and let me tell the House why. The cost of education is not going down. It is going up. Salaries of teachers and professors are going up. These salaries have to go up; otherwise the teachers and professors would not be able to meet the cost of living because the cost of living is going up. The cost of equipment for our universities is going up. Almost every type of equipment purchased by our high schools and universities today costs more than it did three or four years ago and much more than it did in 1977. Books are costing our libraries more money today, excessively more, and they have to be purchased; but there are going to be fewer books purchased and consequently our students will have less access to the wisdom of the world.
What is very serious, as far as I am concerned, is the quality of education for the people generally. It is not right and proper today to provide education only for the rich of this country. Some of the highest positions in Canada today are held by many who were born into poor homes; some of them were in my classrooms in school. They hardly had enough to eat through the Depression years but their parents sacrificed and worked so they could get an education. They went out and found jobs and by dint of hard work they were able to get an education. Some of them today are holding the highest positions of reponsibility in this country, in our churches, our economic life and our political life. They were able to do that because they were able to get an education. However, those men and women, had they not secured that education, would be on our relief rolls today or standing in a bread line, as many young people are doing today.
I quote from a recent article in Maclean's magazine:
In 1981, according to Statistics Canada, 3.5 million Canadians were living within its definition of poverty. In 1982 the number jumped to 4.1 million. The 1983 figure, which will not be available until Fall, will probably be roughly 4.4 million.
There are 4.4 million people living within the Government's own definition of poverty, and that is something of which no country can be proud. Yet when we reduce the amount of money for our universities and educational facilities, we will
Established Programs Financing aggravate that figure. There is no way we can do other than aggravate it because, in the first place, more and more of our young people will not be able to go to university. I know what that means. I would have liked to be a doctor. When I was a young man I yearned to be a doctor. But I came from a family of 10. My father was a hard-working man but he could not find work in the Depression years. My brothers worked hard in the coal mines and by dint of sacrifice they managed to send me to normal school and to university for one year so I could teach school. That was all they could do. My father passed away, some of my brothers married and had responsibilities of their own, and I took on the responsibility, along with other brothers, of looking after our mother and younger members of the family. In my case, university was out of the question because of economics.
I went to school with scores of other young people who could not afford to go to university and so the contribution they could have made to this country was lost. They had great ability, much greater than some of the rich boys in our class, and much greater than even I thought of having, but they were denied their opportunity. Their potential was lost because they were unable to get to university, not because of a lack of ability but because of a lack of money. It should not be so hard for our young people to get into university.
The federal Government started a program of assisting post-secondary education but now it is going to withdraw to a degree and leave it up to the provinces. That will be hard enough on the rich provinces but it will be very tough indeed on the poorer provinces. That is not fair to young Canadians. We talk about a standard in this country that we want no Canadian to live under, but what will happen to the maritime provinces which have little resources compared to Alberta, British Columbia or Ontario? We are simply telling the young people in the maritime provinces that they are going to be handicapped for life because they cannot go to their own excellent universities. That is not right. This Bill is wrong in principle because it is denying our young people the right to an education.
I enjoyed the comments made by the Hon. Member for Beaches (Mr. Young) regarding the deaf and I could not help but think about the blind and the handicapped, those in wheel chairs and those who were born as slow learners, not stupid but slow learners. What are we going to do about these people? It takes extra money to teach the handicapped. I was proud one day to step into an office in the City of Calgary where I was greeted by a lady in a wheel chair. She had gone through university and was holding her own with everyone in that office. I felt glad to be a Canadian. But we are condemning people who are slow learners, who are blind, who are deaf, who are handicapped, to a life perhaps of poverty. Perhaps they will be part of the 4.4 million people below the poverty line which Maclean's magazine spoke about. That should not happen just because they were not born to parents who have a million dollars, although I do not begrudge these people their money. They probably earned it. But I certainly do not appreciate the fact that those who come from poor homes are going to be

Established Programs Financing
condemned to poverty for all their lives because we deny them an education.
When I was just a kid I talked to a preacher from a foreign country. I was complaining about having to go to school. He said to me that I was a very lucky young man. I could learn to read and write. I could reach almost any apex I wanted to reach if I had the ability and worked hard enough. In the country where he was a missionary, very few boys and girls learned how to read and write. They would give their right arm just to be able to read. Yet here in this country, this rich country with all its resources, we are saying to our young people: "You are condemned to poverty because we will not provide the facilities for education. In fact, we are cutting them down". We are applying the "cube root". How can we face our young people and tell them we are going to help them get work and then refuse them access to education?
The Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Roberts) has been advertising courses in newspapers, but when young people go to apply the employment office does not know anything about it. I was at a meeting in a place called Brogg Creek. Someone told me he was interested in improving his education and he saw this advertisement in the newspaper, which must have cost the Government a considerable amount of money, but when he went to the employment office they knew nothing about this program. I wrote to the Minister asking about this but have not yet received a reply. Maybe there is an explanation. However, we spend money advertising and building up the hopes of people. It is the same with programs under UIC. How many scores of those who want to cannot get into the training classes because the quotas are used up?
The Hon. Speaker is showing me one finger. That means I have one minute left. I had wanted to speak in detail about the native people of this country. In Gleichen there is a school called the Old Sun College. It is a wonderful college. It is fighting to get enough money to keep its head above water. It is a college that will give Indian boys and girls an opportunity to compete. In Drumheller there is the Votex Training school for the subnormal. I was in that school the other day. Eighteen people aged 12 or 13 up to 50 are learning to make things. I was proud of the fact that they are no longer on welfare, as they would have been. Now they are making toys, benches and tables. They can do it if we give them the opportunity. We have a tremendous country. We have tremendous resources and tremendous people. Let us make sure that every one of them has an opportunity to reach his or her greatest potential.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it would appear to me that the Government is very conscious of biblical obligations. It looks as if it were establishing in perpetuity a memorial to the statement: "To him that hath
shall be given and from him that hath not it shall be taken away". That is exactly what we have in the Bill before this House at this moment in time.
I would first like to address in general the remarks made by the Member for Gloucester (Mr. Breau). He was the Chairman of the parliamentary task force in federal-provincial fiscal arrangements. In response to what he has said I would say that that task force made recommendations across the board which have been ignored and denied in section after section of this Bill. Any attempt to justify this Bill by any remarks of the former Chairman of that committee seems to me to abdicate the responsibility which he and I both have with respect to our province and to other provinces in a like position.
For instance, he has continued to follow the Government's policy of pulling blindfolds over the Canadian people in respect of the $190 million which appeared to be a windfall at one moment in time in Atlantic history. That $190 million which he has described in his remarks, the details of which I shall not go into, was as a result of, and has been repeatedly stated to be as a result of, a miscalculation of federal statistical authorities. As a result of that miscalculation the Atlantic provinces were short-changed in payment in the years concerned. The $190 million has not been advertised by the Government and its speakers as a statistical error at the federal level, but rather it has been trying to expand upon the great largess of the Government of Canada as it relates to the Atlantic provinces. That is misleading, inaccurate, inappropriate and inexcusable.
No matter how the Member for Gloucester wishes to dabble in extraneous statistical material to arrive at the conclusions which he expressed in his remarks, it just does not wash with reality. This Bill is contradictory to the total principle of federal assistance which has been necessary for those have-not provinces of Canada as described by Justice Emmett Hall in his study. The established programs financing was introduced as a block fund and the financial data are reported in this manner. The expenditures include all spending on health-related and post-secondary education programs as agreed to by a joint federal-provincial committee.
Federal contributions include the cash transfer of established programs financing plus federal contributions for health care received under the cost sharing arrangements. The established programs financing tax transfer is not reported as a federal contribution because these taxes are collected under provincial law. It is the provincial government and not the Government of Canada which takes responsibility for raising these revenues.
I would like to give you some statistics, Mr. Speaker, in respect to the impact of the block funding structure and the funding arrangements agreed to in 1977. Provincial expenditures on health care and post-secondary education in 1977 were $345.3 million in New Brunswick. In 1982-83 they reached $712.2 million. When the cost was $345.3 million the federal contribution was $123 million or 35 per cent. This escalated until eventually in 1979-80, under the agreement of 1977, the federal Government had reached a level of 41.1 per
April 10, 1984

cent of the cost of the cost-shared programs in New Brunswick. This was up not quite 6 per cent.
Since the new trend has taken place in federal budgeting and since we have decided that we are going to save money, the decline has amounted to exactly 12 per cent of provincial expenditures supplied by the federal Government. The total expenditures for the province have more than doubled, from $345 million to $712 million. The federal contribution has not quite doubled. It was $123.7 million and is now $207.6 million. At one point in time it was 41 per cent of the cost of those provincial expenditures. It is now 29.1 per cent. No matter how you cut this cake, when you cut 12 per cent of the expenditures of the province from federal allocations to the province you have dealt it a crippling financial blow.
This does not deal totally with post-secondary education as this Bill is supposed to, but that is only part of the pie. The first major federal-provincial cost-shared program was hospital services. This program, introduced in 1958, provided for the federal Government to cover about one-half of the cost of approved federal services with the provinces covering the other half. In the late 1960s the medicare program was introduced. Here again the federal Government agreed to cover on average-please note the phrase "on average"-half the costs of provincial medicare programs. The average implied that there should be recognition of those provinces with less economic capability than others.
I was a member of the provincial legislature of the Province of New Brunswick when hospitalization was introduced. At that time it was agreed that the federal Government should accept something in excess of 60 per cent of the total cost of hospitalization for the Province of New Brunswick. Likewise, when medicare came in the federal Government shared in excess of 50 per cent of the cost of that program. I guess the provinces were smarter than the feds; they estimated more accurately the needs of the provinces than the federal Government estimated its expenses for the programs which it had structured.
Having underestimated the cost of these programs, in Bill C-12 the federal Government is now trying to transfer to the provinces that are beleaguered by financial problems, as is the federal structure, more of that expense. Those provinces cannot afford that. While the suit can be cut to fit the cloth year after year, eventually some part of the financial body will be naked. That is what will happen if this Bill begins a perpetual trend in the fiscal responsibilities of the federal Government as they relate to the provinces.
The third major cost-shared program involved federal grants for post-secondary education. In 1967 the federal Government offered to pay the provinces 50 per cent of the operating costs of post-secondary educational institutions, or $15 per capita. New Brunwsick opted for the $15 per capita.
The original arrangement worked quite well through the 1960s but the problem began to emerge in the 1970s. The provinces were having difficulty coping with the rigid program
Established Programs Financing and spending guidelines laid down by the federal Government. Those guidelines that were set by the federal Government displayed an effort to influence provincial politics by federal expenditure through the power of the purse. It is a betrayal of the relationships which should exist between the Parliament of Canada and the provinces.
The provinces were having difficulty coping with the rigid program and spending guidelines laid down by the federal Government which, in many cases, directed provincial spending to high-cost rather than less expensive program areas. The federal Government was concerned about the open-ended nature of its financial involvement in which it had to match provincial spending. However, the Government still wanted to guide how that spending should take place.
Beginning in 1972, the Government began to take steps to reduce its financial commitments when it placed a cap on its contributions for post-secondary education. The introduction of caps and ceilings was absolutely contrary to the intention of the original agreement.
In 1977, federal arrangements replaced federal conditional grants to the provinces in support of medicare, hospital services and post-secondary education with a new program called Established Programs Financing. Again, that worked favourably for the provinces until there was a 6 per cent increase in the share borne by the federal Government. The provinces out-foxed the federal Government because they knew more about their needs and anticipated requirements than the federal Government.
Once that plateau was reached the program at the federal level started to go downhill again. We cannot afford to let this happen. Once a standard in any social sphere is established, one must be very cognizant of the fact that someone will be embarrassed if that standard is cut. The intent was to embarrass the provinces and it is unacceptable for the Government of this day not to fulfil its responsibilities by backing away from the costs of a program which it prescribed.
The Established Programs Financing was set up. According to this program a single cash grant and a transfer of personal and corporate tax points replaced the cost-sharing arrangements under which the federal Government helped to finance medicare, hospital services and post-secondary education. With EPF, the federal contributions were no longer determined by the provincial program expenditures, as they were before. It was no longer the set percentage of provincial expenditures; they were tied to the rate of growth in Canada's economy. This gave the federal Government greater certainty about its financial commitments. Of equal importance, it placed upper limits on its financial obligations. This less attractive financial arrangement was made acceptable to the provinces because the federal Government assured them that EPF would give provincial governments more flexibility in program decisions.
I have sat in the House and listened to the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss Begin) in particular, enraged in her ideology, demean the provinces about their expenditures in a contemptible way. Yet the intent of this

April 10, 1984
Established Programs Financing
program was to get the finger out of the pie of provincial management. That was the understanding.
The provinces were asked to seek ways and means to gain more effective control of the expenditure of provincial and federal money. Let me quote the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau). He said:
(EPF) ... suits the current and future imperative, namely fiscal restraint, in that provinces will have a greater incentive to implement what are admittedly difficult measures designed to restrain spending in these fields to reasonable levels.
That is a statement by the Prime Minister. This meant that the provinces were free to manage their own affairs without political or financial interference by the Government of Canada. They were able to govern themselves under their own circumstances. For the most part, the provinces favoured the move to EPF, although it was recognized that, particularly after EPF was phased in, provincial costs for medicare, hospital services and post-secondary education would grow more rapidly than federal contributions. The provinces recognized this from the beginning.
One of the key features of the EPF arrangement was that it was designed to produce long-term certainty for both the federal and provincial governments. The federal Government obtained certainty that no matter how much the provinces spent on these programs, its contributions would not exceed the growth in the national economy. The provinces obtained certainty that the federal Government would refrain from applying arbitrary caps and limits to its contributions, and so could plan accordingly.
This Bill is in absolute contradiction of the federal-provincial negotiations which were presumably carried on in good faith. In fact, limitations are now being imposed as a result of withdrawing funds from the field to which we were so committed and which the Prime Minister addressed in such a very positive fashion.
Established Programs Financing worked fairly well from 1977 to 1982. However, over that period and within the last year, the federal Government has done much to destroy the principles upon which EPF was based. It has launched counter-productive quarrels with the provinces and caused serious distrust between the provinces and the national Government.
Less than two years after it convinced the provinces to accept the EPF arrangement, the federal Government wanted to change its terms and thereby reduce EPF payments to the provinces. On this occasion the provinces successfully resisted those attempts but the federal Government responded by cutting other transfer programs and terminating discussions for a new block funding arrangement for social services. It terminated those discussions and applied other financial pressures.
In the 1981 federal Budget, the Government announced that it planned to cut over $5 billion from EPF funding over the period 1982 to 1987. This cut was implemented in the spring of 1982, contrary to the recommendations of all the provinces, the Economic Council of Canada and an all-Party parliamentary task force chaired by the Hon. Member for Gloucester
from New Brunswick. In 1983, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde) announced that federal EPF contributions would be arbitrarily capped in so far as post-secondary education was concerned.
In view of the remarks made by the Hon. Member for Bow River (Mr. Taylor), we must consider the consequences of capping post-secondary education expenditures, especially at a time when virtually every Minister of the Crown is saying that the Government will promote more training. However, this legislation will ensure that it is not done at the post-secondary education level, since its financing will be capped. That is precisely what this legislation will do.
The Province of New Brunswick spent over $700 million on these programs in 1982-83, or approximately 29 per cent of its total Budget. Against this, the province received about $200 million from the federal Government for health care and post-secondary education.

That means a province which has 70 per cent plus or minus the national average income of this country has to impose nearly the highest taxes of any province in Canada to support post-secondary education and other policies in that province. The people of New Brunswick may not pay as many
April 10, 1984

dollars per capita as people do in Ontario, British Columbia, or in Ottawa Centre, but a bigger portion of their income is going in provincial taxes, no matter how you try to cut the pie. It is a bigger proportion. The burden on the people of New Brunswick is relatively heavier than in other provinces.
Let me come to the Province of Newfoundland. A Cabinet Minister in Newfoundland stated on television this morning that Newfoundland's average income was 52 per cent of the average national income. That means that in the Province of Newfoundland people are labouring even harder and sharing the widow's mite even more than the people in New Brunswick. These things are not recognized. If I had one reason to criticize the federal-provincial task force, it would be because the task force was made up in its total not with the Member for Bow River, who has provincial experience, not with the Premier of Prince Edward Island with his provincial experience, but it was made up of a group of people who had never participated in and were not, with all due respect, as familiar with the problems of provincial budgeting as were other Members of this House. No Party appointed a single Member to that committee with that background. I submit to you, Mr. Speaker, that the conclusions of the report, though very very firm and definite, were coloured by the lack of knowledge, experience and understanding of the difficulties which Atlantic Canada perceive, and which are real.
This Bill is in contradiction of Emmett Hall. It is in contradiction of the task force. It is in contradiction of the statements made by the Prime Minister of Canada when the EPF block funding program was brought in. I want to point out to you, Sir, that it is a ceiling on how much the federal Government will pay post-secondary education. Regrettably it is not the floor; there is a variable which makes it possible for an application of less than the six and five ratio of increment and expenditure, which is mentioned, but the little dog-eared section down there states that under certain statistical conditions we do not have to increase that payment even by 5 per cent. We might increase it by 2 per cent, 3 per cent, or 4 per cent on an annual basis. All this is contradictory to the means of the provinces of Canada, particularly Atlantic Canada.
I wish I had time to quote, but I will not abuse the unanimous consent I received. I refer Members of this House, including the sarcastic Member from Ottawa Centre, to Emmett Hall's statement about the need for additional federal help for post-secondary education rather than make cut-backs in the extension of federal grants for health, education, and welfare. His statement unequivocally says that if and when this happens there will be a reduction in the quality of services in an area of Canada which, even at the time of the Emmett Hall report, could not meet the standards of Canada. Instead of less, Mr. Justice Hall was recommending more.
Bill C-150 was in this House. It never reached second reading. In the interests of humanity, of education, and of the taxation incapabilities of Atlantic Canada, I pray that this Bill will never come to third reading and a vote in this House of Commons.

The intention was to reduce the federal commitment and at the same time raise the profile of the politics of the contribution. New Brunswick, I may say in response to the Hon. Member, cannot afford a drop of $10.3 million in post-secondary moneys which are granted for two reasons. This is because a great many people go from other parts of Canada to the Atlantic provinces for college education, at least to the bachelor level. This is fact.

Canada, particularly to the Maritimes, than it would be to any other area of Canada for that purpose.

subtopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL FISCAL ARRANGEMENTS AND ESTABLISHED PROGRAMS FINANCING ACT, 1977 MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext: Or grandmother teach granddaughter.

subtopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL FISCAL ARRANGEMENTS AND ESTABLISHED PROGRAMS FINANCING ACT, 1977 MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
As my good friend reminds me, or grandmother teach granddaughter. From year to year the nature of what we need to know changes rapidly, and change in education demands a much greater commitment to education.
There was a period of time in our history when I was but a young boy starting school and the local vernacular in that rural farming community was that one needed grade 9. Somewhere during the early periods of my schooling, I heard parents discussing around farm kitchen tables that grade 9 was not good enough any longer and that one needed grade 12. Unfortunately, about the time I reached that grade it should have been utopia but people were saying that it was no good any longer and that one needed university education.
We are into a new age today where there is no such concept as termination of education. One does not reach a certain level and say that is it for life. One does not train to become a doctor and say: "Now I am a doctor for life". At least, I do not want any medical treatment from a person who graduated ten years ago and that was the last he ever read about medicine. Today education is continuous and ongoing. There should be no end to it, even for our senior citizens. I have been thrilled in my constituency on many occasions when I witnessed persons over the age of 70 years who had less than a grade 12 education but through extension programs had the opportunity to attend university.
We are talking about an enormous range of importance. On the other hand, the Government of Canada is cutting back from the federal domain payments to the provinces for 198384 of $118 million and for 1984-85 an additional $260 million. What is important is that it establishes a new base by which the Government can say in future years that from that original platform it makes its calculations into the future. The federal Government, which established a program of block funding to the provinces, has taken the position of establishing a new lower base. We will either have a situation of poor education forever, a greater burden on the provinces or a greater burden on individuals.
This is the age of the microchip. It is an age where education ought to be continuous. In one country at least, Japan, the view is that education is continuous. We have entered into a Liberal age of slogans-the land is strong; the just society; six and five. They have not demonstrated to Canadians, certainly not to the two Opposition Parties, that there is six and five less need for education. I have seen no studies, research or material to indicate that we should spend $118 million less this year and $260 million next.

April 10, 1984
Established Programs Financing
We are living in the age of the slogan. We have the slogan of six and five. This Government has bankrupted itself with PetroCan, Canadair, Mirabel and Pickering and other wasteful spending, and is now cutting out education. It is too simple to recognize and realize that education is an investment in the future. If you look at any advanced society, you see a society that is educated. Therefore, slogans such as the just society and six and five do not meet our needs.
We need an in-depth analysis of what our optimum education ought to be and at what levels we ought to expand. Had some commission made an in-depth study of that requirement, we could then accept the numbers more readily. Not only do we not have any research indicating what the levels of expenditure ought to be; we have unilateral action taken by the federal Government. The federal Government entered into an agreement with the ten provinces. It is unilaterally breaking that agreement. It is decreasing the amount of block funding. On the basis of that decrease, it tries through speeches by the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) to pretend that we in this country will have participatory democracy and renewed federalism. How can you have renewed federalism when you have a dictatorial attitude on the part of one of the 11 partners, telling the other ten that it has decided they will get less and there is to be no discussion? There have been no federal-provincial discussions on this matter. The Minister in charge has not travelled about the country to determine what the burden on the provinces will be if the funds are decreased. The Government simply writes out new legislation saying the provinces will receive $118 million less next year and $260 million less the next. It presumes there will be some gratification because when speaking to the Bill the Minister said that less was more.
This is all part of the double-speak of the Government; silk cloth, smoke and mirrors, the magic show of felt hats and rabbits, trying to make less look like more. The Government says that 6 per cent is more than zero per cent, but fails to recognize that it is less than the traditional commitment. It describes it as more when in fact it turns out to be less. The Minister knows that the provinces are not happy. He has not had any agreement with the provinces with regard to this legislation.
More important is what this Bill does. It freezes the ratios into an inflexible straitjacket. We have before us a presumption that the calculations of the federal Government as laid before us today are accurate, that 50.5 per cent should go to hospital insurance, 17.4 per cent to medicare and 32.1 per cent to post-secondary education. If we could make the presumption that the federal Government was correct in those ratios, I challenge any Member on the Government side to stand and argue that they will be the correct ratios for Canada for all of our foreseeable future.
Is it not possible that somehow down the road there may be a breakthrough in preventive medicine and this will result in decreased costs? Therefore, we could shift our ratio to greater needs for education. Is it not possible with the advancement of the microchip that society might advance so quickly that, in
order to get into the mainstream of whatever point the world is at at that time in history, the ratios may need to change?
In 1984 the federal Government would freeze forever a ratio system. It does that on the basis of the national average. That challenges the other presumption. Are we to presume that the ratio needs of Prince Edward Island are the same ratio needs of Alberta? Is Quebec to be presumed to have exactly the same needs in health as that of Saskatchewan?
I challenge one partner in this federation coming up with a set of numbers. It fails on two presumptions; first, in its future implications and, second, in its regional differences. We are in a situation where the amounts of money granted are such that we need to separate those ratios into at least having input on a continuing basis from each and all of the provinces. It was not the prerogative of the Government unilaterally to make the choices, to establish its brand, to claim its need.
In the past, the federal Government issued block funding for a number of social services. It is now running this magic show by us, changing the title of the Bill and breaking that block funding into prescribed measures. The more the feds prescribe, regulate, define and dictate how block funding is to be broken down and spent, the more they intrude into provincial jurisdiction.
The Government may feel comfortable in its heart and soul defining that block funding will not go as a block, but as all of the parts of the block. By the power of the dollar, it will become the administrator of the provinces. If it can control that block in all of its parts and define how each individual part is to be spent, it takes away the flexibility of the provinces to shift ratios toward health or away from education, regardless of whatever the individual provinces may feel is their need.
The federal Government today not only shortchanges education but damages federalism and provincial jurisdictions. It lords itself over the provinces as a powerful central Government which the country ought not to experience.
I do not speak against central governments or unitary governments simply as an automatic reflex. A unitary government may well be a satisfactory form of government in England, Belgium or Holland. However, it is not a satisfactory form of government in a country that is the second largest in the world, stretching from Vancouver Island to St. John's, Newfoundland, some four and a half thousand miles. This is a country that, by its very breadth ahd scope, requires regional input. When block funding is broken into all of its component parts and its spending is prescribed, the result is a federal Government which intrudes in a very direct way in what ought to be and is prescribed by our Constitution as being the jurisdiction of the provinces.
There are those two faults, the federalism concept and the fact that the Government tries to apply a national average to all parts of the country as if all needs were equal. The people who form the Liberal Government are trying to pretend to us that averaging is somehow a satisfactory way to go in terms of a Canadian objective. I will say through you, Sir, to a Liberal;
April 10, 1984

"If you had your head on a firebox and your feet on a block of ice, on average you would feel pretty good". I submit that Liberal members have not recognized the uniqueness of the north, the Atlantic provinces, the western prairie provinces or the West Coast. They have not recognized the different cultural milieux that exist in the big cities and various regions of the country.
To lower funding for post-secondary education is quite literally to lower our income expectations. It is no new fact to anyone in the House that those nations which have a lower standard of education have a lower standard of living. They not only have a lower standard of living in terms of dollars but they have a lower standard of living in terms of the soul of the person. Education provides us with an opportunity to discover our outer limits. It is a chance to find out who we are and what we can become. When we in a society like Canada deny a person, young or old, the opportunity to say yes to the challenges that come his or her way and the ability to say yes to an opportunity to grow and expand, we end up with restricted people with restricted souls. Education is the key that unlocks the universe. It is there for us to discover.
I dare any person to say yes to the challenges that come his or her way. People who say no to challenges, who say they cannot and do not dare to discover new things, live in a rut. A rut is simply a grave with both ends kicked out. Education opens up a new universe and allows us to bombard our own outer limits.
The federal Government's response to the age of the microchip is to say that it will cut back funds for education. I can tell you, Sir, that nothing could be more out of concert with the needs of our time. We are in an age today when the new information that comes to the fore year after year makes obsolete that which we were taught only a short time ago. In a time when there should be an enormous expansion of education, we find that the federal Government is cutting back by literally millions of dollars on its federal obligation.
I ask Members opposite how they justify that perspective when members of their Party are going around the country attesting to their leadership qualities and some of them are saying that there will be zero unemployment within five years. How can there be a zero unemployment rate without giving more funding to education? Surely a look at the world tells us that it is the educated nations which have the opportunities for more jobs. Education must first of all be broad-based. It cannot become elitist. It must not be something only for the privileged.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it seems incredible to me that we are spending so much time on this particular subject when it is so obvious that the Government should be looking at withdrawing the Bill or withdrawing
Established Programs Financing
the portion of the Bill which will affect post-secondary education across the country. This Bill amends the Federal-Provincial Fiscal Arrangements and Established Programs Financing Act. This amendment gives to that Act a new name but it is still the same old Act with only a few variations.
The main purpose of the Bill which is before us is to apply the six and five principle to post-secondary education transfers from the federal Government to provincial governments. The Bill has to some extent taken into consideration the federal-provincial fiscal arrangements task force report, though it has taken very little of that report into consideration. It has considered only those parts of that task force report which it thought would reduce the amount of cash it would have to pay out.
The Bill does follow one of the recommendations of the federal-provincial fiscal arrangements task force report by separating health care funding and secondary education funding from the other block funding. It provides also for a minimum of accountability. I say a minimum of accountability because it only requires that information on the manner in which transfer moneys are spent be tabled in the House. It does not particularly require that all of the transfer moneys which are to go to secondary education or health care be spent in that particular way.
We in the New Democratic Party thought that that amendment should have been incorporated into the Bill. However, the amendment which did pass was taken almost directly from the federal-provincial fiscal arrangements task force report and does require the kind of accountability by provincial governments which would require them to put before the House information about the manner in which the money was spent. In that case, some of the arguments which we heard this morning of the Hon. Member for Ottawa Centre (Mr. Evans) and the previous speaker who comes from New Brunswick should not have taken place. That kind of information would have been before the House.
I must go back to the real purpose of the Bill, Mr. Speaker. I do not understand why the Government would make a move like this at this particular time. The significance of the move itself is obvious; it will take approximately $378 million from post-secondary institutions across Canada in the next two years. Part of that reduction is retroactive; it is money that the institutions have already committed or have spent. What is probably more important is that the $260 million being taken from 1984-85 will establish a base for future payments to secondary education. Surely there has not been a reduction in the need for education. If anything, the need has been increased by the recession, the downturn in employment. People are looking for new ways to make a living and education can help them find new directions.
The amount of money the Bill establishes will govern the kind of education which post-secondary institutions are able to put before the people who need it so badly, the people without work. If we do not give the money to the institutions-I do not

April 10, 1984
Established Programs Financing speak only of universities but community colleges and technical institutions, which also come under the Bill-then people's ability to find a job will be affected.
The costs of education are increasing, therefore the funds provided by government must also increase. Reducing the money that the federal Government pays forces the institutions to cut back on existing programs and not create new ones which would provide the kind of education required to make people feel a little more secure in the future.
It is all a question of priorities. The Government has decided to save money in the area where it is easiest to do so, and that is the transfer of funds to the provinces for post-secondary education. If that money is cut off the effects will be felt this year, next year, the year after and for many years to come, but it could be done immediately without drastic effects. A few thousand students would not get into the programs they choose and for another few thousand the programs that would equip them for jobs in the future would not be available. This result will be felt three or five years from now.
For a long time the Government has been saying that its priority is employment and that it is going to spend millions of dollars to provide jobs for the youth of the country. Then almost in the same sentence it suggests the kind of restraint which would not allow youth to train for those jobs.
Training programs will be important for youth during the next few years. It is not as if the federal Government had accepted the idea that it does not have some responsibility in education-which many of the provinces would argue is the correct decision-that it does not have responsibility to provide training. Over the years the federal Government has accepted the responsibility and has made many incursions into the training field. That started with training for World War II. A lot of training was necessary at that time and the Government undertook it. After the war, with the huge development that took place after 1945 and in the early 1950s, the federal Government developed institutions and provided per capita grants for training which was directly related to the jobs that were available.
After the war we had to go to the European countries and even to South American countries to find people with the skills that we wanted and which were necessary to help us develop as a country. Because there was a great need for training at that time the federal Government took its responsibility and got into the training field. It did so through direct capital grants to help build the institutions that were necessary and through per capita grants for the number of students actually in training. It made changes and put the money where it was needed. Later it backed off that decision and instead of paying a per capita grant in 1977 moved to block funding which would allow it to operate on a formula. The basis of that formula was that it should be able to give the provinces and the federal Government some idea of the amount of money available for education in the next year or the year after. That was a base which everyone recognized.
What has happened is that the federal Government has changed the base and will not increase funding as it has in the
past. It will reduce the base from that of two years ago, the percentage increase will be reduced and will not be that which was agreed upon. Instead of taking into consideration the need for training and the need for flexibility among people, the Government decided to reduce the amount of money available for education. That will make it less possible for our youth and older people looking for jobs to get the training they need.
It is easy to reduce the money paid to colleges and universities. It seems that in the process you are not making some kind of priority decision, but in the long run that is exactly what you are doing.
May I call it one o'clock, Mr. Speaker?

subsubtopic: FUNDING OF OTTAWA MULTICULTURAL WOMEN'S CENTRE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am at a loss to understand the actions of the Department of the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Roberts) in deleting $45,000 from the funds of the Ottawa Multicultural Women's Centre. This money, Mr. Speaker, is needed to rehire badly needed co-ordinators for the Centre in order to maintain and improve programs to assist immigrant women in the important task of adjusting to the Canadian way of life. As is well known, Mr. Speaker, immigrant women do have special problems in this area and badly need this assistance.
To cut off a program which is needed and is proving successful, is another example of the total absence of common sense. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, I call upon the Minister of Employment and Immigration to reconsider this decision and restore the cutback to the Multicultural Women's Centre. Failing this, Mr. Speaker, I would ask the Minister of State for Multiculturalism (Mr. Collenette) to take a serious look at this problem with the view to filling in the possible void if no action is taken by the Deparment of Employment and Immigration.
April 10, 1984

subtopic: ALLEGATIONS MADE BY QUEBEC MINISTER OF EMPLOYMENT
ALLEGATIONS MADE BY QUEBEC MINISTER OF EMPLOYMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, speaking before the National Assembly recently, Quebec's Minister of Employment referred to the pilot project designed to help ablebodied young people under 30 and stated that, if such a project is not really worthwhile, it is due to the federal yoke and that independence is the solution.
Mr. Speaker, that is a false and misleading allegation. Indeed, the Quebec Minister of Employment came to Ottawa to discuss this program with the Minister of National Elealth and Welfare (Miss Begin). With enthusiasm, we accepted to share the costs of that program for which, incidentally, we will be paying $59 million over two years. This is in addition to the $924 million given to Quebec for 1983-84 under the shared cost social assistance program.
Mr. Speaker, it is utterly ridiculous to make the people of Quebec believe that, if they foot the bill by themselves it will cost them less than it does now when we are paying 50 per cent of the cost. If anyone is forcing Quebecers to carry a yoke, it has to be their provincial Government which is driving them towards independence against their will.

subtopic: U.S.S.R.-CONDEMNATION OF OFFICIAL'S PRAISE FOR DOWNING OF KOREAN AIRLINER
U.S.S.R.-CONDEMNATION OF OFFICIAL'S PRAISE FOR DOWNING OF KOREAN AIRLINER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, through their many barbaric acts the Communists have made clear their utter disrespect for human life. During the first 30 years of Soviet dictatorship, 83 million people were murdered. In Afghanistan, communist troops have slaughtered entire tribes and have gassed innocent civilians. And, of course, we can never forget, nor forgive, the downing of Korean Airlines Flight 007, in which 269 innocent passengers were thoughtlessly massacred by the Soviets.
These murders are only an example of their savagery. Their pride in their repulsive violence is even more indicative of their cruel nature. In the Soviet Union, Sunday, April 8, marked the official "Day of Anti-Aircraft Defences", hailing the downing of the Korean jetliner. A senior Soviet military official stated the destruction of the plane was a feat of arms comparable to the shooting down of the American U-2 spy plane in 1960.
For these reasons, we will never be able to disarm unilaterally, nor can we ever trust the murdering Communists in disarmament, or even disarmament negotiations.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Leader of the Official Opposition (Mr. Mulroney) proves what we have been saying for months. His address in support of the linguistic minorities is nothing more than an attempt to put Canadians to sleep. His actions contradict his words. First, he has never denounced the anti-French Members for Winnipeg-Assiniboine (Mr. McKen-zie)and for Simcoe South (Mr. Stewart). Second, he has never told the Manitoba Members who refused to be associated with the motion in support of francophones in that Province to toe the line. subtopic: CALL FOR ACTION ON COMMITTEE RECOMMENDATIONS
CALL FOR ACTION ON COMMITTEE RECOMMENDATIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the New Democrats call upon the Government to act quickly and positively upon the 80 recommendations listed in the parliamentary report, Equality Now. In recent public briefing sessions held by members of the Special Committee on the Participation of Visible Minorities in Canadian society, we often had comments raised about the injustices done to Chinese immigrants who had to pay head taxes of up to $500 per individual.
The first Chinese immigrants to Canada arrived in 1858. From 1885 to 1947, along with several other discriminatory measures imposed against them, they had to pay a head tax. Historical documents estimate that between 1886 and 1923 the federal Treasury was enriched by $22 million from the head tax levied only on Chinese immigrants.
We in the New Democratic Party call upon the Government to recognize this injustice and see that those who suffered in this disgusting manner are duly compensated.
In the report, Equality Now, considerable concern was expressed about the lack of advertising by the Government in the ethnic media and the visible minority media. Advertising is the life blood of the ethnic press. We urge the Government to

April 10, 1984
respond to these concerns instead of basically using the Main Street dailies to communicate with the various ethnic cultural groups.

subtopic: MEETING WITH MEMBERS OF THE UPA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, UPA representatives met with several members from Quebec and the Minister of Agriculture this morning. The UPA representatives hailed from various areas in Quebec and the discussions dealt mostly with the disastrous spring of 1983.
Mr. Speaker, the Minister of Agriculture confirmed to the UPA representatives that he was willing to consider their requests for compensation for the losses they suffered provided these request are channelled through the Quebec Government as required by the rules of the game. In other words, the Minister is willing to consider the requests for compensation, but not under any condition. Requests must be made through the Quebec Minister of Agriculture, Mr. Garon, and I urge him to listen and to meet with the federal Minister of Agriculture as soon as possible to discuss this serious problem in Quebec.

subtopic: TREATMENT OF FEMALE CANDIDATE BY COMPETITION BOARD
TREATMENT OF FEMALE CANDIDATE BY COMPETITION BOARD
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, despite the introduction last fall of another phase of the affirmative action program which was to ensure that discrimination against hiring women for middle and upper level positions within the Public Service would be abolished, the Government is still only paying lip service to recognizing and fully appreciating the abilities of Canadian women.
An example of how well this affirmative action program is working was vividly brought to my attention. A well qualified, competent woman was insulted and degraded during an interview for a rather unconventional job opportunity in the Public Service. She was told by a member of the interviewing board that she was only there as the token female candidate to satisfy Treasury Board's affirmative action post board scrutiny.
This woman knows she has the right to take her case to the Human Rights Commission, but will not do so for fear of jeopardizing any chance she has with future competitions for which she has applied. How many more women are there in this same position?
When confronted with this kind of neanderthal attitude toward hiring women, how can the women of this country believe they will be employed as a direct result of their ability and professionalism, and not because they are required to fulfil
an insulting and degrading quantitative goal the Government opposite hopes will secure the feminist vote? Mr. Speaker, we in the Conservative Party know full well the meaning of affirmative action for women-that merit and not tokenism should be the only factor considered in the assessment of a woman's ability to fill a position. When will the Government opposite stop treating 52 per cent of Canadians like second class citizens and a minority?

subtopic: CALL FOR COMMITMENT TO FULL EMPLOYMENT POLICY
CALL FOR COMMITMENT TO FULL EMPLOYMENT POLICY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it appears that the Conservatives are giving some attention to the report of the task force on employment opportunities. At their seminar last weekend at Mont Ste. Marie they proposed, among other things, that there be tax deductions for educational and training savings. That was recommendation No. 88 of the task force report. Most of the other reported proposals on employment training were likewise taken from the task force report.
While the Conservative action is welcome, I would be even more enthused if they and the Liberal leadership candidates supported recommendation No. 1, to implement a full employment policy, and recommendation No. 2, to establish an industrial strategy linked to employment and training policies.
Oral Questions
Full employment is possible, Mr. Speaker, if there is a political will to achieve it. On the two occasions since World War II when Liberal Governments made the commitment, in 1945 and in 1964, unemployment was reduced to 3 per cent between 1946 and 1953, and to 3.8 per cent between 1965 and 1967. Mr. Speaker, let us have a six and five program for unemployment to reduce unemployment to 5 per cent by 1986.

maintopic: ACHIEVEMENT OF BARGAINING RIGHTS FOR EMPLOYEES
ACHIEVEMENT OF BARGAINING RIGHTS FOR EMPLOYEES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think it is important to comment on the fact that the House of Commons has just been invited to take another small step into the twentieth century. Members of Parliament will be aware that 15 years ago the parliamentary committee on employer-employee relations in the public service recommended that employees on Parliament Hill be granted bargaining rights similar to other public servants. Many Members will also be aware that Governments since that day have refused to grant those rights to the employees of Parliament. Unfortunately, it is not to the credit of Parliament that these rights are now becoming a reality.
Great credit, on the other hand, must be given to the Public Service Alliance and to the Canada Labour Relations Board. The Labour Relations Board has issued a ruling that employees of Parliament fall under the Canada Labour Code, as we have suggested they did for years, and that Parliament cannot prevent this by harking back to the centuries-old tradition of parliamentary privilege.
This is indeed a great day for the employees of Parliament who have now been granted the rights other Canadians have taken for granted. Mr. Speaker, at the conclusion of Question Period, I wish to address two points of order. I think these points of order are important to the ability of the Official Opposition to question the Government properly and effectively with respect to its policies.
My first point of order, Mr. Speaker, deals with your interim observations with respect to the questioning of the Minister of State for Economic Development (Mr. Johnston) about a particular Crown corporation. I believe that two elements must be considered before we make any definitive decision about the ability of Members to address questions of an economic nature to the Minister of State for Economic Development. It may be that these questions related to a specific Crown corporation policy but you will have to understand, Mr. Speaker, that the Minister responsible for that Crown corporation is in the other place. The Minister responsible for the CIDC is in fact the person who would have prime responsibility for that Crown corporation. When asking direct questions relating to the administration of the Crown corporation, we are precluded from asking the Minister who has direct responsibility.
I would like to point out that on that basis alone, we should be given some reasonable latitude to deal with Ministers with economic portfolios who, I think it would be fair to say, have the responsibility of supervising and directing the activities of Crown corporations. Indeed, referring to Petro-Canada by way of example, it is a matter that is well known and has been stated by the Government that Petro-Canada is an instrument of government policy. It is a window on the industry but it is primarily an instrument of government policy. The Government has indicated to us over and over again that this Crown corporation in particular was, as my Leader has said, one of the engines of economic activity in our country.
I do not believe it is reasonable to attempt to restrict us when directing legitimate questions about the policy of the Government to the Minister who has specific responsibility for economic development. Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point of order. I regret that the Minister for International Trade (Mr. Regan) has left the House but I feel it is important to raise the matter now in order that you may consider it, Mr. Speaker.
You are aware, Sir, that on page 115 of Beauchesne, Citation 327(1) reads as follows:
A Minister of the Crown is not at liberty to read or quote from a despatch or other state paper not before the House, unless he be prepared to lay it upon the Table.
Citation 327(5) reads as follows:
To be cited, a document must be quoted or specifically used to influence debate.
You will know, Sir, that during the Question Period my Leader asked the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) a question with regard to some actions that were being undertaken in Central America. The Prime Minister yielded to the Minister for International Trade for the purposes of answering. In the process of answering the first question asked, the Minister for International Trade made a direct reference to, and I believe cited from, a document which he claimed was a communication between the Government of Canada and the Government of the United States with regard to this very important matter.
I would ask you, Sir, carefully to review the record in Hansard to determine whether my understanding of what was said at the time is correct. If I am correct and the Minister did in fact make reference to and use that particular document in an effort to influence the proceedings at that particular point in time, I would ask that the Minister be required, as per the generally accepted practice not only in this House of Commons but in the House of Commons at Westminster, to table the document that he used to influence the conduct of the proceedings.
