You commented very briefly, Mr. Speaker, that he had a valid point. I would like to argue for a moment that it is a valid point only in a very limited sense.
While it is true that Mr. Speaker Jerome did not allow Parliamentary Secretaries to ask questions, it has always been
Privilege-Hon. J. Munro
my belief that Mr. Speaker Jerome was wrong in making such a blanket ruling because a Parliamentary Secretary has a very limited responsibility to the House and a very limited influence on Cabinet Ministers. In fact, that responsibility and influence pertains only to the particular Minister to whom he is Parliamentary Secretary.
It is my contention, Sir, that it is not proper to deny the right of a Parliamentary Secretary to ask questions of other Ministers. It should be taken for granted that he or she would not ask questions of the Minister to which the Parliamentary Secretary is assigned. However, to prevent a Parliamentary Secretary from asking questions of other Ministers of the Crown to whom he has no attachment and for whom he bears no responsibility whatsoever is, in my opinion, denying that Parliamentary Secretary a right which is provided to every other Hon. Member of the House except Ministers of the Crown.
I can see no justification for denying to a Parliamentary Secretary the right to ask a question pertaining to his constituency or to Government policy matters for which he bears no responsibility whatsoever.

subtopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL FISCAL ARRANGEMENTS AND ESTABLISHED PROGRAMS FINANCING ACT, 1977 MEASURE TO AMEND

speechtext: The House resumed consideration of the motion of Mr. MacLaren (for Mr. Lalonde) that Bill C-12, an Act to amend the Federal-Provincial Fiscal Arrangements and Established Programs Financing Act, 1977, be read the third time and do pass.

subtopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL FISCAL ARRANGEMENTS AND ESTABLISHED PROGRAMS FINANCING ACT, 1977 MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I was commenting before lunch on the priorities of this Government as far as education is concerned. Basically, the point which we have been trying to get across to the Government in suggesting that it withdraw either the six and five clause from this Bill, or the Bill entirely, is that it recognize the effect its action is having on the educational system in the country.
It is easy to reduce the amount of money that is being given to colleges and universities. However, what is the effect of not having the funds available? How does it affect universities in the country? The youth are probably the most dependent upon post-secondary institutions-the technical schools, universities and other institutions-of education. They are going to be unable to get the kind of training they think is going to be necessary. It is going to affect the kind of medical research that is going on. It is going to affect the development programs of the country which are so important to Canada. It is going to affect research in agriculture. In the case of agriculture, Mr. Speaker, we need 100 new researchers for the next two years to replace those that are leaving the service and to bring the service up to standard.
All of these are the effects of the Bill that is before the House. It indicates a kind of short-sightedness, Mr. Speaker, which we are getting used to with the Government. However, we would expect that in this particular area the Government might have taken a second look.
What happens if we do not have funds to finance educational institutions? If we do have those funds available we are able to build a flexible work force which can fill the jobs which will become available during the next few years. Everyone knows and accepts the fact that almost all of the people in the major industries will have to be retrained in the next few years. If we have the funds we can guarantee that there will be a work
force in the future that can fill the jobs that are available. People will also have the opportunity to expand their horizons. We have programs of continuing education and retirement education. You can name almost to no end the kind of programs that can be put forward if the money is available. Instead of that, the Government is reducing the amount of money that will be spent on post-secondary education or transferred to the provinces to be passed on.
What happens when funds from the provinces are not available for education? In that case we will have many less skilled workers available. We will have less people available to teach at universities. We will be forced to go overseas or south of the border for instructors at universities. If the cycle that took place in the 1950s and 1960s repeats itself, by 1990 we will be looking overseas for skilled labourers to fill the jobs available in Canada.
Right now we spend almost $1 billion per month on unemployment insurance payments. Part of the reason for that is that we do not have jobs. When we do not have the money to invest in education, it affects the whole standard of education across the country. The Government is inflicting an on-again-off-again restraint program on the educational system. We are never really certain what funds are going to be available next year. That makes it impossible to start programs because it is not known whether they will be completed.
Many other countries use the opportunity which comes from unemployment to upgrade the standard of skill of their workers. Sweden, for instance, has a very good system. It gives at least 4 per cent or 5 per cent of its unemployed people the training they need. We must realize, Mr. Speaker, that money spent for education is wisely spent. If we continue to spend it we will be making an investment in the future and guaranteeing a good future for many more people. It is not a waste of taxpayers' money. It is an investment which can train a whole new generation of Canadians. Undue restraint is a waste, Mr. Speaker. It reduces the opportunity for people to fulfil their potential.

Mr. Speaker, I have been listening to the remarks of the Hon. Member. I have great concern about this subject. One of the things that bothers me is that not only are we seeing moneys reduced from what they otherwise would have been, but we are seeing this practice extended into the future. I would like to have the Hon. Member's comments with regard to the projection for 1984-85. It is bad enough that funds are being taken out of this current fiscal year that would otherwise have been transferred to the provinces. However, that is also being projected forward so that next year there will be some S260 million less sent to the provinces for post-secondary education than otherwise would have been the case. This is happening at a time of crisis in the university situation.
April 10, 1984

I would like to ask the Hon. Member for his comments on whether that $260 million should at least be set to one side. The Government is going ahead with the current year, but surely it could consider the 5 per cent limitation it is putting on the next fiscal year and decide not to take that decision at the present time. The Government could let that part of the Bill go and change its mind about that. How could the Hon. Member react to that suggestion?

subtopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL FISCAL ARRANGEMENTS AND ESTABLISHED PROGRAMS FINANCING ACT, 1977 MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the Member's question. As the Member has mentioned, we recognize that the present reduction of $118 million is for the past year. The universities and post-secondary institutions are already missing that money because they had planned on spending it. Anything the government could do to replace that money or guarantee to provide the $260 million for 1984-85 would be very helpful. Of greater danger is the fact that we are projecting this base for later years. Therefore, we will be reducing the total amount of money that will be spent relative to what we are spending now. From past experience we know that by 1990 we will be looking overseas for people that we should be training now. If we do not get the money back very quickly we can expect that to happen and there is not very much we can do about it.

subtopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL FISCAL ARRANGEMENTS AND ESTABLISHED PROGRAMS FINANCING ACT, 1977 MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext: There being no further questions or comments the House will proceed to debate. The Hon. Member for Calgary West (Mr. Hawkes).

subtopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL FISCAL ARRANGEMENTS AND ESTABLISHED PROGRAMS FINANCING ACT, 1977 MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, for the first time since I have been elected to the House of Commons, I wish to make a speech in French today. It is a special occasion for me after the many lessons I took in that language.
Last weekend, the caucus of the Progressive Conservative Party had a challenging debate on technology. At the end of that debate, we issued a press release. In that release, we mentioned that the Progressive Conservative study group on labour technological reconversion and recycling had concluded that Canada does not have the tools required to come to grips with tomorrow's technological challenges with respect to training and recycling. According to the members of the study group, the problems of the last decade stemmed in part from the fact that the Government's investments in human resources fell short of the mark. That is the major problem in our country. I repeat the last sentence: the Government's investments in human resources fell short of the mark. It is a serious problem, and the subject under consideration today is along the same line, since we are talking about the country's human resources in secondary schools. The Government intends to cut down its investments in that sector and I think that, in this day and age, it does not augur well for Canada.
Mr. Speaker, it is also stated in the release that, unless there is a significant increase in resources earmarked for training, we will end up with far too few workers with the skills required
Established Programs Financing to meet the future needs of the labour market. Therefore, the study group urged the Progressive Conservative Party to make major changes in current policies and programs so that workers will have better opportunities to improve themselves. Our young people need more challenging opportunities to better themselves, but in the present context, Mr. Speaker, the same thing applies to adults because they are the ones who ought to attend secondary level courses lest they be left behind in this rapidly changing world. All Canadians have a stake in this issue.
On that occasion, the Leader of the Official Opposition (Mr. Mulroney) said that the recommendations contained in the report would make training and recycling more readily accessible to those who need them, while at the same time ! providing for a better mix of private and public funds to achieve our goals with respect to training. I am referring to the release, Mr. Speaker, but the report itself contains 24 very important recommendations for the country.
We came to the conclusion that Canada is facing five major problems. We said that the first one is the need to make industry and labour more aware of the opportunities offered by new technology. The second problem is the urgency of redefining national policies with a view to promoting increased productivity in the public and private sectors. The third one is the need to upgrade and speed up our methods of gathering, processing and circulating statistics related to the labour market. The fourth and most important problem in my opinion is the need to increase financial and human investments in the field of education, to extend the training programs available in the private sector, to update the existing public educational facilities, to upgrade the teaching profession, and to look for new ways to provide the necessary training. There are many concepts to deal with in the area of education. Each and everyone in the public sector needs funding, and this is very important in today's debate. The fifth problem is the need to promote co-operation between governments, industry and labour.
Mr. Speaker, the Progressive Conservative Party has suggested that for the well-being of all Canadians our national policies must be changed in five major areas. The first thing would be to change the taxation system so as to promote investments in the field of education by encouraging individuals and businesses to invest in the development of human resources.
The second change would be to provide better opportunities for welfare recipients to take part in programs which would help them acquire new skills for the future.
Mr. Speaker, the third change would be to increase the role played by the private sector, by businesses and non-profit organizations alike, in providing training services.
The fourth change would be to develop policies to promote the acquisition of new skills and their use to manufacture new products, and to make this approach the cornerstone of an

April 10, 1984
Established Programs Financing industrial strategy directed toward the future. The fifth change would be to revamp some of the systems and institutions in our society in order to promote co-operation and reduce the conflicts between governments, labour and industry. These are the five major concepts related to policy changes in Canada. These are major concepts developed to solve major problems. In each case, they are very important concepts related to education in Canada.
Mr. Speaker, we have made 24 specific major recommendations. The first one is to provide financial assistance to people undergoing training. Among the types of assistance which could be available would be financial support provided by the employers and the Government. There would be various ways to provide this support, but the Task Force has suggested the following:
(i)	All persons eligible under public assistance programs (including unemployment insurance, social welfare or Workmen's Compensation Board benefits) should be allowed to take training courses while receiving benefits, even under programs that are not sponsored by the Government. These programs should also be changed to establish clearly that the major purpose is to develop human potential first and foremost. They must therefore last as long as necessary to allow the trainees to acquire the skills which will make them less likely to find themselves in need of financial assistance in the future. It would be important to invest in the area of human resources.
(ii)	The people concerned must be encouraged to invest in their own development. There would be many ways of making this easier for them:
(a)	By authorizing the development of tax-free savings plans which could be used for educational purposes. If we provide tax savings for people who put money aside to buy a house, we should develop a similar investment plan for them to improve their skills. It would be the same as for housing plans.
(b)	Tuition fees should be deductible from income, whatever its source. Education is an investment for the individual, and the Income Tax Act should be amended accordingly.
(c)	Many individuals who are greatly in need of training have very little money and often hardly any assets.
For them to be able to invest in their own training, a sort of loan system would have to be set up. These loans would have to be guaranteed if they came from the private sector. The current student loan program could be considerably extended for this purpose. On the other hand, we could consider establishing an education mortgage plan, guaranteed or insured by the private sector.
It is suggested in paragraph (d) that the Unemployment Insurance Act should be thoroughly amended to emphasize employment instead of unemployment. Benefits should be paid to the people who are really trying to fit in the labour market,
to develop their skills, increase their mobility, obtain the necessary counselling and training, if they lack the knowledge and experience they need to compete on the labour market. Amounts paid for unemployment insurance purposes should be considered not as expenses, but rather as tax credits aimed at compensating for current inequalities. People who have contributed to the scheme for long periods of time without ever applying for unemployment insurance benefits should be entitled to longer eligibility periods for re-training purposes.
Paragraph (e) states that the Income Tax Act should be amended to encourage employers willing to do so, to offer financial assistance to their employees who wish to seek full time or part time training. All relevant expenses should be considered as tax deductible items. Moreover, they should receive tax credits to compensate their costs.
Mr. Speaker, I think that the public school system needs teachers to teach adults: it is very important for the future. Today, we are dealing with a bill calling for the reduction of the amounts paid for secondary education. It is quite the opposite of what we propose. In my opinion, Mr. Speaker, Bill C-12 is very bad for this country.
In our report, Mr. Speaker, we deal with illiteracy, but its Section C is very relevant to this debate. We refer to extended educational opportunities. These are major policies for this country.
The first recommendation in this section is as follows: A new government should immediately commit itself to encouraging the purchase of the most sophisticated school material, by contributing a subsidy equal to any investment.

subtopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL FISCAL ARRANGEMENTS AND ESTABLISHED PROGRAMS FINANCING ACT, 1977 MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is not my custom to speak very often on debates of high finance or intricate economic measures. It is not my field of expertise. I do not pretend to be an expert on it. However, I have had a dozen years of experience in post-secondary education, so I have an interest in what is going on in this debate.
The first point I would like to make is that the debate in which we are now involved is probably the most eloquent statement we could make against the kind of regime we are experiencing in federal-provincial involvement in higher education. It is the experience of all of us that we represent communities and agencies in our constituencies which depend upon government grants for their existence as a way of life. That in itself is an excruciating experience for these agencies. They are dependent upon the whim or the caprice of the funding agency whether it be municipal, provincial or federal.
April 10, 1984

For any worth-while organization to have to predict the caprice of a funding body is a tortuous experience for it regardless of how well intentioned is the funding agency or the organization depending upon the grant.
Second, it points to the wisdom of our founding fathers that the federal Government has its area of major occupation and attention, that the provincial governments have theirs and that under the BNA Act the provinces are responsible for education because they are the most intensely affected by it and can most precisely represent their needs. There is a great deal of wisdom in that. However, some decades ago we moved into a new regime whereby we initiated federal-provincial transfer payments. The provinces under that agreement, because those transfer payments appeared to be very attractive and met the immediate need of all governments for funding, agreed with the new regime or the new system. It seems to me that it is an unfair balance because under the federal area of responsibility, there is a disproportionate amount of power when it comes to granting systems. The federal Government has taxation abilities which provincial and municipal governments do not have. Therefore, it has a capital pool which it can use to manipulate and manage its programs. Also it has the capacity to print money. Fortunately, there has been a tapering off in that activity recently, but it has the capacity to inflate the currency and, therefore, do an injury all the way down the line.
We have a situation where the federal Government can design a package and introduce it, as it did two decades ago, a package which is very attractive to the provinces in the funding of the medical and educational services and which the provinces like, particularly the have-not provinces which have a real need for funding if they are to maintain a level of medical or educational services that is equivalent to that in other provinces. It becomes very attractive and they go for the bait, but once they are hooked, they are hooked. Once they have taken some grants and get into a five-year program of funding, as this kind of legislation provides, what do they do at the end of five years if they decide it does not meet their needs? By that time a dependency has been created. It creates a dependency which, after a while, becomes unattractive as much as it becomes necessary to the provinces or to the institutions within the provinces. The provinces within their areas of jurisdiction are capable of retaliation or at least try to counterbalance what is going on in the federal Government. They are jealous of its powers.
The federal Government has begun to take an interest in education in the provinces over the past several decades and takes a very paternalistic view of the provinces when it says, "Obviously you cannot handle it; we will give you a hand". The provinces realize that constitutionally education is their prerogative. It is their right to design educational packages to meet the needs of their people. Therefore, they want to guard that power and that jurisdiction as carefully as possible, but they feel the squeeze because while they have fairly extensive taxation powers, they are not the same as those of the federal Government.
Established Programs Financing
We are facing what many of us on this side of the House warned the Government about in 1977 when it decided to become involved in block funding. Originally the agreement with the provinces was that there would be an understanding on how the money would be spent. For some curious reason in 1977 the Government decided that it would move to a new system of grants-block funding. It was to give the money holus-bolus to the provinces and let them administer it. We on this side of the House said that we did not think it was a very good idea.

Second, while Hon. Many of the problems we face today are not created by legislative disagreements or disagreements regarding areas of jurisdiction or accountability. They are attitudinal problems. When a new government is in office representing the nation, there will be a new attitude in federal-provincial relations.
I can tell my friend, the Hon. Member for Gander-Twillin-gate (Mr. Baker), that at that time there will be no pejorative overtones when our federal Ministers go to the provinces to settle disagreements. Surely we must be mature enough federally to get over all the pejorative overtones to which sadly, we have become accustomed in our federal-provincial relations until now. We can recognize that mature federal and provincial jurisdictions can have areas of honest disagreement without resorting to paternalism, name calling or strong-arming.
I would like to tell my hon. friend that calling for accountability of the provinces to the federal Government is no different from the provinces calling for accountability of the municipalities. Provincial governments make grants to municipalities and other agencies within the provinces and they understand
Established Programs Financing
that when they grant money to other jurisdictions within the provinces, they have a right to know how that money is being spent. They are not calling those agencies dishonest but they are calling them to account. They are simply asking them how the money was spent. That is what bothers me about my friend's question. As soon as we ask for accountability, members of the Government want to turn it into something pejorative. It is not an accusatory request but simply a logical question of competent accounting.
Sometimes people make mistakes, a mistake is not necessarily a crime. If a provincial Government has misspent some money in the eyes of the federal Government, that is not criminal, but it does call for an accounting. I see nothing wrong with that.

subtopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL FISCAL ARRANGEMENTS AND ESTABLISHED PROGRAMS FINANCING ACT, 1977 MEASURE TO AMEND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to participate also in the debate on Bill C-12, an Act to amend the Federal-Provincial Fiscal Arrangements and Established Programs Financing Act, 1977. In my Province of British Columbia, Mr. Speaker, a lower emphasis is placed on universities than in any other province. Over the last ten years, spending in this area has fallen from 10 per cent to 3.5 per cent of the provincial budget. In this context the federal Government is pushing through a Bill which will retroactively limit to six and five federal contributions earmarked for post-secondary education. I can just imagine the glee with which the Government of British Columbia will point its finger at the federal Government with regard to the cutbacks in education in the province. However, the fact remains that there are serious problems in the Province of British Columbia and that that right wing conservative Government-and that is what it is-has struck out in these areas.
There has been a massive outcry against the closing of the David Thompson University Centre in Nelson, British Columbia, My colleague, the Hon. Member for Kootenay West (Mr. Kristiansen), has explained very accurately many of the implications of this move on our area of the country.
There is a further implication which I would like to spend some time discussing. That is the fate of the East Kootenay Community College. This college is a young institution and the only post-secondary educational institute in the East Koote-nays. It was built because it was recognized in more progressive times that educating our young people is a laudable pursuit and also an investment with a substantial payback.
We have seen the outright attack on the David Thompson University Centre in Nelson, British Columbia, and I think it is appropriate at this time that we should identify what this Party has tried to do with respect to the implementation of funds from the federal and provincial Governments. The New Democratic Party placed an amendment which read in part that any such cash contributions for hospital insurance, medical care programs and post-secondary education programs should be expended in the provinces for the purposes of those programs only. And, Mr. Speaker, although the Conservative Party had brought forward a substitute amendment which it feels is satisfactory, we feel that this is the only way in which we can ensure that that money is going to be spent for education so that there is equality in education in British


April 10, 1984

Columbia, Alberta, and right across Canada. We are not going to get this with the kind of frivolous amendment put forward by the Conservative and Liberal Parties.
Naturally, we must support this provision as second best, but the amendment put forward by the Hon. Member for New Westminster-Coquitlam (Ms. Jewett) would have addressed the problem in a very serious way and ensured that the moneys would only be spent in these areas.
We saw in the early 1950s when the Bennett Government, that right-wing conservative Government, brought forward a program of 3 per cent sales tax. That was supposed to help pay our medical and hospital costs in the Province of British Columbia. Not only has it been increased from 3 per cent to 5 per cent and as high as 7 per cent, they are now bringing in another tax of 8 per cent over and above that in our taxation system. That is the kind of policy which the right-wing conservative governments right across Canada are bringing about.
We heard the Hon. Member for Bow River (Mr. Taylor) talk about his concern for education. Alberta has literally billions of dollars in the Heritage Fund. If it is really concerned about education, why does it not step out to the front and show us some programs for the blind, the elderly and the handicapped such as the Hon. Member for Beaches (Mr. Young) spoke about?
A headline in one of the newspapers in British Columbia reads, "Students demand school before coal". An amount of $2.5 billion of federal-provincial money was poured into the northeast development of the coal fields in order to provide coal which we already have in the Kootenays and which we could have shipped to other countries. But $2.5 billion was spent in northeast British Columbia, and therefore 1,250 miners in southeastern British Columbia were laid off during peak times. That is not good enough. If we are going to make investments, let us make investments for the future of our country. Let us make an investment in our youth so that they are able to go to universities. What did the Minister for the Province of British Columbia say about the theme of northeast coal versus higher education? He said that more money for schooling would have to be borrowed. One of the students said, yes, the Government should borrow for education, pointing out it is doing exactly that for its other projects.
We must prepare ourselves for the realities of the 21st century. What happens in our post-secondary institutions, our vocational and technical schools, colleges and universities has never been more important. At a time when we should be investing more private and public money in training and education, what are we doing? Countries such as Sweden, Japan, West Germany, and Austria are investing more and more of their private and public money in post-secondary education and training. But if you look around the world you will find one country which stands out, in a sense, for cutting back on post-secondary education, and that is Canada. If that is not a step toward committing not only economic but social suicide, I do not know what it is.
It is reported, Mr. Speaker, that one of the most pressing and long-term problems which we in my riding will have to
Established Programs Financing
face is whether the East Kootenay Community College can continue to operate the satellite campuses which are considerably more expensive. Similar programs would have to be located at Cranbrook. I put it to the Liberal Government and its Tory friends that if this Bill is passed, satellite campuses operated in Kimberley, Golden, Creston and Invermere might have to be shut down. People in these communities are going to hear about it and the Tory and Liberal candidates are going to have a hell of a time defending their Parties' records on this matter. In the field of art and culture it is important that these community colleges be able to reach out to people in these rural areas to give them the opportunity to expand on their skills and programs.
There is another local issue which relates to this Bill. In Cranbrook we have a very innovative Energy Action Centre. This particular centre is well established. Its reputation is excellent. For a number of years the centre has provided many educational campaigns with respect to energy saving. The funding for the centre from the Department of Energy has ended. It was hoped that the program being offered at the Energy Action centre would be incorporated into the curriculum at East Kootenay College. The idea was well received. What better way to ensure the continuation of valuable community resources than by hooking up the centre with the community college? In fact this is the whole idea behind the flexibility of the curriculum of community colleges. The idea has been scuttled by the East Kootenay Community College board of directors for fear of funding cuts emanating out of Victoria and implicit in this Bill.
The Hon. Member for Beaches spoke about the needs of the handicapped, the underprivileged and the blind. In the Province of British Columbia the right wing conservative Government has cut one of the basic programs which was starting to recognize the needs of the blind. The Ministry of Education withdrew a $50,000 contract from the Crane Library at UBC to provide talking books for blind students. Shame on that right wing Government that, without any heart or feeling, decides not to carry on with such programs!
It is imperative, Mr. Speaker, that we have some form of mechanism in place to ensure that when federal moneys are made available to the provinces for post-secondary education, medicare or anything else, there are guarantees that the moneys are used in those areas. Sixteen of the seventeen Conservative Members of Parliament from British Columbia stood up in the House and voted against guarantees that those moneys be used for post-secondary education only. I can only say that people of British Columbia had better take a very serious look at what these Conservative Members are doing. We have a serious enough problem in British Columbia with that provincial Government without adding insult to injury on the federal-provincial scene.
I would like to speak a little bit more about what is happening with the David Thompson University Centre in Nelson, British Columbia. My colleague from Kootenay West,

April 10, 1984
Established Programs Financing
whose riding adjoins mine, has explained the ramifications of the shut-down of that university. The ramifications can have very serious effects on the funding that is made available to the East Kootenay Community College and the inability to accommodate the people of that area.
I would like to mention some of the good work that went on there. In Rossland they started a program especially for young women to enable them to learn to operate heavy machinery in the mining areas. It qualified them for employment in the coal fields near Sparwood. These kinds of programs were needed and were starting to take place. However, the province of British Columbia has turned its back on them. Young students coming out of high schools and wanting to attend UBC or Simon Fraser University are going to find that tuition fees and costs are so high that they will not have the same opportunities as people living in the urban areas. This is wrong, Mr. Speaker. It is outright discrimination by a Government that does not recognize its responsibilities. Unless the federal Government and this federal House ensures that there are some guarantees that the money will be spent on various programs, we are not going to have a universal education system across Canada. We are going to have a block of provinces deciding their own priorities for education. That is not good enough. People in all provinces should have the same opportunities. No province should have the right to use that money for something else because of economic hardship.
That is what this debate is all about, Mr. Speaker. We cannot accept that. We are opposed to what is happening here and what has already happened to British Columbia. This program is retroactive to March of 1983. Can you imagine what is going to happen to the educational system in B.C. when this Bill is passed? I welcome the opportunity to get on the election platform in British Columbia and debate this subject with the Conservatives as well as with the Liberals. They should be ashamed of themselves. In a country as rich in resources as ours is we should not be debating whether our youth are going to have an opportunity to have equal education across Canada. Mr. Speaker, this is not good enough. When I hear the rhetoric coming from the Conservative Party it almost makes me sick. It almost makes me sick to sit here and hear about their grandiose plans when I know full well what they are doing in each province. What they are doing in British Columbia should not happen anywhere in the field of education. If there was an ounce of gumption in these Members of Parliament they would be holding a task force on education in British Columbia and coming back here and demanding some rights, instead of going out to look at the procedures of the income tax department. Did their task force come back and say that CP Rail should pay all of its deficits? No way will they touch that.
We have a very serious problem in the field of education, Mr. Speaker. This Bill is not going to answer that problem. I for one am very opposed to, and not very proud of, what is happening with regard to this piece of legislation.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I suspect that during the past ten minutes we have had inflicted upon us a type of 11 per cent Amos and Andy performance on matters that are really irrelevant to this particular Bill. The previous speakers were dealing with a local issue, which undoubtedly is very important to the people involved, but one might think that the Hon. Members from the Kootenays were playing prairie politics as far as this particular Bill is concerned.
This Bill is an extension of a philosophy which was imposed upon Parliament by a Liberal administration since 1977 and which has zapped the medical care programs in many provinces and placed the post-secondary educational budgets of a number of the provinces in grave difficulty. If the Hon. Members from the Kootenays think that their regions are particularly hard hit, I suggest that they should get their noses above the ground to see some of the other areas of the country that are equally affected by the suppression or limitation of educational institutions whose benefits to the community are marginal when compared to the cost of keeping them.
During boom times people are quite prepared to tolerate these additional expenses, but it is different when a budget must be slashed and costs must be cut. Those Hon. Members are the underwriters of the philosophy that if one borrows, begs or steals enough money to throw at a problem, it will go away, the Liberals have had the same philosophy in the last few years.
This Act has passed the second reading stage. No amendments may be put, other than a time consuming amendment to
Established Programs Financing return the Bill to committee for the examination of a certain clause. We cannot even give it a six-month hoist. I believe I share the views not only of Canadian educational commentators but of those from abroad who have examined the current state of Canada's educational system. Quite frankly, I believe we suffer from over diversification. The Constitution provides that education shall be a provincial matter and goes so far as to provide a council of educational ministers. This council will not even let a Minister of the Government of Canada attend its conferences as an observor at the same table, even though the federal Government spends almost $7 billion a year on education in various forms.
When one considers education through the Armed Services, the payments that are made according to this Act and through other means, such as through the Secretary of State, these education oriented moneys mount up. However, the Government of Canada has no more to say about it in the national determination than does any one of the provinces. Consequently, we see the provincial authorities taking different approaches and adopting some rather odd standards. These policies stem either from tradition or from the current fashion, but there is no national goal for education. My colleagues in the New Democratic Party as well as other colleagues talk about the changing requirements of our educational standards, that these must fit in to prepare people not for today's requirements in industry, but five years, 15 years or 25 years down the line. It is notorious that the Canadian workforce, be it clerical, supportive, administrative or in various trades, is ill-equipped to meet the exacting standards of a competitive world. We stand there in many instances merely wringing our collective hands about what might be done, about what ought to have been done, instead of thinking about what we are going to do about it now. This particular Bill is a clear example.
I do not know what I can call the attitude here in Canada with regard to education. We have universities that maintain different levels of qualifications. We have different professional bodies that maintain the idea that the wheel was invented in their particular jurisdiction and that they must pass on it. We have trades-testing bodies in the various Departments of Labour in each of the provinces which must sit and examine each worker coming from another province to validate that person's work ticket. In French I would say:

-it sounds like the Tower of Babel!

-because you get these conflicts. But we get the same conflicts in school. Has anyone ever tried to transfer a postsecondary student from one of the western provinces into Quebec or Ontario? We will leave alone the PQ nonsense about language and so forth. That will go away-

-and as soon as possible, because this is another one of the complexities of the Canadian system. In any case, Mr. Speak-

April 10, 1984
Established Programs Financing er, we must create this atmosphere of co-operation between the Provinces, that have jurisdiction over educational matters under the Constitution, and the federal Government, that has a basic interest in providing a national purpose or philosophy for the educational system in Canada. The federal Government will have to come to terms with the Provinces. Then, it might be possible to eliminate some of the problems which this Bill will actually emphasize.
I do not like this Bill at all because it imposes increasing restrictions on the funds to which the Provinces are entitled. It is as if the federal Government owned all incomes in Canada as of right. We know that this is not true. The federal Government acts as a collecting agent and then distributes the money among the Provinces in accordance with a formula accepted by the governments concerned.

You know about these unilateral changing of agreements. It happened in 1977 and again now. The provinces have not been consulted and we are telling the provinces what they can do with their own money under the agreements and outside the agreements. But that is the arrogance of this over-centralized Government. It has been as clear as spring water as we go along that this is merely-if I may mix my metaphores- another slice of salami off that sausage, and before long we will see the Government of Canada laying claim to all revenues. In philosophy it does in the tax department, or shall we say the tax policy department of the Department of Finance- and I invite my hon. friend, the Parliamentary Secretary to examine it.
The basic theory under the Government's tax equity policy is a buck is a buck is a buck, and as soon as a dollar is earned, whether by an individual or a corporation, the Government of Canada is entitled to a certain percentage, and it wants it now. Whether the Government is entitled to it all is another question. It must share taxes with the provinces for which the Government collects a part. Some of the provinces collect all their own corporate taxes, and Quebec collects its own income tax, but not entirely. What had been a good practice in the past is now degenerating, again because of the over-centralized philosophy of the Government of Canada. Those provinces that feel strong enough to break away when they cannot get an agreement, some form of co-operation, naturally will pull out. And the reaction of federal Cabinet Ministers? Well, they fashion a new noose, put it on tighter, thanks to a supine majority that refuses to examine the implications of the law and what they are doing to their own provinces. I do not doubt for one moment that one of the reasons we have not experienced it as they have in the Province of Quebec is the attitude of the Quebec Members in this House who work against the interests of that province in supporting the Government without a word or a murmur of protest against policies which are contrary to what should be the best regional interests in the country.
We have the same thing here. The Canada Health Act is the other half. It imposes stringent limitations on the provinces
where the provinces have the right under the Constitution to the administration of Canada's health services. But what does the federal Government do? It says: "You cannot do that."
