SOCIAL AFFAIRS
subsubtopic: ADVISABILITY OF EXAMINING MEASURES TO PREVENT MARRIAGE BREAKDOWN
speechtext:
That the Standing Committee on Health, Welfare and Social Affairs be empowered to examine and enquire into the incidence and effect of marriage breakdown, its social and economic implications, its effect on government programs and policies, and, in particular, without limiting the generality of the foregoing, to recommend measures to prevent marriage breakdown and strengthen the institution of the family, and for such other measures in the same matter as the committee may consider desirable.
He said: Mr. Speaker, once upon a time young Canadians entertaining thoughts of marriage dreamed of the proverbial
April 10, 1984

little white house surrounded by a picket fence and beautiful children, but as Bob Dylan said, "The times they are a-chang-ing". The times have changed and so has marriage. This March, Statistics Canada told us that 40 per cent of Canadian marriages now end in divorce, and for young Canadians under the age 25 years, the shattering news is that nearly one of every two marriages ends in breakdown.
There are many lessons we can learn from the erosion of marriage and the human tragedies that are represented by the cold statistics. Eminent social philosophers like Erich Fromm point to the enhanced influence of material and commercial values in our culture, and suggest that they have begun to permeate our most intimate social relationships. Christopher Lasch sees the media fostering desire for novelty and instant satisfaction as a form of societal neurosis which undermines commitment at every level. Today, individuals no longer find it necessary to enter into a marriage to be sexually active, to have a social life or even to have children. As a corollary, many people no longer find it necessary to remain in an unsatisfactory marriage to achieve these same goals.
The strongest support for the institution of marriage, the family, and its preservation has traditionally been the church. To a considerable and regrettable extent, the influence of the church has diminished and, by the same token, a sacramental and covenantal view of marriage has diminished along with it and been succeeded by a more secular notion, with more marriages performed outside the church and more couple entering marriage with equally high ideals but without the guidance of the church or marital counselling.
The women's movement of the 1960s and the 1970s which stressed individual rights and human potential has often been scapegoated for some of the profound status changes in roles within the family. Critics point to the fact that in 1948 only 26 per cent of married women with school-aged children worked outside the home, while in March of 1976, 54 per cent worked outside the home, most of them full time. However, this ignores the economic facts of life, which in many cases mean that if junior is to have a good time, proper clothing, be well nourished and educated, both partners are required, not always by choice, to enter the world of work. Pursuit of separate careers has been a divisive force in some marriages, but in other cases where partners work at helping each other develop as persons, adjustments have been made and successful marriages have resulted.
Out of the upheaval and turmoil of changing times in the last two decades, it is becoming apparent that the role of the housewife and mother deserves special recognition and a new respect. Changes have taken place in marital property laws and pressure is finally mounting for long overdue improvements in tax and pension legislation as well as a measure of economic independence.
Clearly marriages between partners who regard each other as equals and work toward helping each other develop as persons is a positive attitude prevalent in successful marriages, particularly where the roles of the partners are determined by
Marriage Breakdown
themselves before the knot is tied instead of by an unwritten code based upon what others before them have done.
While the technological revolution that has reawakened the reindustrialization of America has produced greater mobility and greater economic vistas for men, it has also presented an economic independence for women that has paralleled the attainment of greater sexual freedom. Effective birth control, acceptance of child-free marriages and marriage-free child raising have greatly altered expectations concerning possible life options. The very wealth of possibilities has introduced enormous challenges to traditional assumptions concerning marriage and family values. Spouses who find themselves taking opposite sides on value-related issues face great potential turmoil.
Many teenagers make the greatest decision of their lives, the decision to marry, with very little or no education in healthful living, interpersonal relationships or marriage itself. Lacking income stability and a mature sense of direction and goals, many teenage couples find themselves saddled with responsibilities and obligations for which they are not ready. Those who enter into marriage in the flush of romance without sufficient time to establish ties of genuine friendship and to ensure mutual values, expectations, habits, needs and goals, are particularly vulnerable to marital stresses. Often what was thought of as love vanishes quickly and resentment over having lost freedom or been denied a normal courtship, coupled with economic and social pressures, may contribute to marital tension and ultimately precipitate divorce action. In such cases the proximity of support of family and friends is often crucial in determining whether the marriage is able to survive and grow. Geographic mobility, often for advancement, has also removed partners in faltering marriages from the stabilizing influence of friends, parents and relatives to new communities and new stresses.
! While it may be true that in temperamental terms opposites attract and that marital compativility is ideally complementary rather than merely supplementary, statistics tell us that extreme dissimilarities and background generally make for high-risk marriages. Attitudes, interests, habits and expectations are largely determined by background influences of family, culture, religion, education and social class. Even when those influences seem to have been rejected, they frequently re-emerge in later years. A person who enters marriage with someone of profoundly different orientation, secretly hoping that his or her spouse will change, is very often disappointed. On the other hand, couples who share strong goals and a mutual commitment in spiritual and moral values have statistically a much longer likelihood of marital success. Loving the same things would seem to be a positive goal.
A frequently cited cause of marriage breakdown is the feeling of dominance or control which one partner allegedly exercises over the other, such as the refusal to see each other as true partners. Women have complained that their husbands feel threatened by any expression of desire for personal growth such as working, taking educational courses, handling money or deciding when or where to spend the family vacation. On

April 10, 1984
Marriage Breakdown
the other hand, men speak of feeling used or maniputaled by their wives' very dependency, being rules by weakness or in other instances of being undermined challenged or demeaned by suspicions. In many instances, these are illustrations of a lack of communication both before as well as after marriage, a failure to recognize character or personality faults in a mistaken belief that they could be changed. This same failure to communicate often prevents couples from profiting from potentially helpful intervention such as marriage counselling or therapy. Divorce petitions are often interspersed with allegations of suspicion, lack of interest, low self esteem, feelings of inadequacy and sexual dissatisfaction. These problems, like career immersion by one or both partners, are normally consistent with dissatisfaction at other levels and generally poor communications in all areas of marriage. As one petitioner put it, he had five years of marriage and three years of hell before the marriage was dissolved by divorce decree.
Clearly we must accept the inevitability of marriage breakdown as a social evil and work to decrease its incidence. Through education we must help people discover a vision of what marriage might be and develop an overall multifaceted program to foster and help the marriage relationship. This, however, is not as easy as it seems. In our western culture, we think of education in intellectual terms, that is the transmission of ideas or objective knowledge often removed from the experience from which it first came. In other words, we do not think of education in terms of values, feelings, visions and dreams, and yet it is in this broader sense of education that we might help young people make the greatest decision of their lives for which today many of them are eminently unprepared.
What do we have to do? First, we have to find a way to help people discover how to develop normal healthy relationships, and then find ways to help them have realistic expectations of a healthy marriage relationship. That means that we will have to develop some sort of personal values educational program so that people can fit their expectations in marriage to what they really want out of life.
Solid family life is important to society. If it is not there, society pays the price financially. There are no accurate measurements in dollar terms in the cost to employers, to the individuals involved or to taxpayers through social support programs, but with nearly one marriage in two going down the tubes, the figure would be mind-boggling. Clearly, our society would benefit greatly even if we did some seed things now to reduce the incidence of unhappy marriages. Recognition of the social value of a family in placing great value on the art of successful parenting is a major step in elevating the status of a family. While attempting to do something on its own, government and the media should discover what is being done to preserve good marriages and support fragile ones, support what is being done well and promote what is being done well.
A lot of what is being done is being done by our churches, but as society becomes more secularized, a large body of people are not able to avail themselves of these opportunities,
and they, too, have a right to a happy marriage. Therefore, the Government and the media should publicize and attempt to encourage programs to support happy marriages within community organizations like university adult education programs, night school programs and programs put on by voluntary organizations. It is important that we do what we can to ensure that support for marriages is universally available. It is socially and financially to the advantage of Canada and Canadians to do everything possible to promote the dignity of marriage and happy families.
When marriage breaks down, the dignity of marriage is not served by trivializing divorce. On the other hand, the present adversarial style of divorce proceedings demeans marriage as well. It is no answer to merely redefine marriage so that it means nothing, like a non-binding commitment or, on the other hand, to enforce legal continuation of that which is already dead at the core. We need new constructive efforts to support marriage and the family in all its forms.
I have attempted to indicate a direction in which we can move to strengthen marriage and the Canadian family, which is the bedrock of our nation. There are other directions. There are programs and there are policies that can and must be developed. It is important that thinking Canadians from every walk of life put their heads together and collectively do the very best we can to strengthen and support the Canadian family.
That is why I proposed this vehicle in the motion now before the House. Whether my views or better ones are adopted is really not important. What is important is that we address the greatest social problem facing Canada today and provide the best solutions that we as Canadians working together can develop.

subtopic: SOCIAL AFFAIRS
subsubtopic: ADVISABILITY OF EXAMINING MEASURES TO PREVENT MARRIAGE BREAKDOWN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we have before us a motion that the Standing Committee on Health, Welfare and Social Affairs be empowered to examine and inquire into the incidence and effect of marriage breakdown, its social and economic implications, its effect on government programs and policies, and, to recommend measures to prevent marriage breakdown and strengthen the institution of the family.
I welcome the motion before us today. It addresses an extremely important problem. It is very timely that we should be discussing it at the same time as the Divorce Act is before the House. We are all acutely aware of the problem of the increasing divorce rate in Canada.
It is very clear that one of the effects on government programs and policies of family and marriage breakdown is the enormous cost that is put upon the state. As a result of families breaking down, there are two households, which cost more than one. We know the large number of maintenance orders which are not paid. There is a need for families to go on welfare. There are increased costs because of income tax deductions when maintenance and alimony are paid. There are increased costs to the state in social services, counselling and
April 10, 1984

all of the intervention services to support people in need whose marriage is breaking down.
I want to look at the social and economic conditions that have probably contributed a great deal to the increase in marriage breakdown. We are in a period of recession. We like to think we are coming out of it, but we certainly have very high unemployment. This causes enormous strains for the family. There are reports from social workers of increased child abuse, wife beating and alcoholism as a result of people being out of work.
Work is extremely important to people, apart from the fact that it puts a pay cheque into the family income. It has a lot of psychological and social significance. People receive fulfilment through work. They find work interesting. People have social connections through work. It is an integral part of life. When people in the prime of life are denied that opportunity, it causes crises in families. It is unfortunate that people in the prime of life are denied work. It is unfortunate that people under stress take it out on those who are close to them and weaker than they are. For that reason, we have to look at very long-term solutions. It is not just counselling that will help people through a crisis, although we certainly need counselling.
Until we have full employment or something close to it, there will be people in crisis, and that will put a strain on marriage and the family. If we really want to put people first, we must have policies designed for full employment. That means a number of changes, which obviously I do not have time to go into now. My Party stresses them in terms of a longterm industrial strategy which puts people first and provides jobs. Jobs are important for dignity and self-fulfilment.
I welcome the role of the church in indicating the importance of jobs for people and full enjoyment of life. I am pleased to see that in the Catholic Bishops' statement and the Pope's recent encyclical on labour.
If we are not able to provide jobs for everybody, the state has a very important role to play in providing a safety net to see that those who are not able to work at a particular time and lose their jobs are not absolutely destitute, that they have unemployment insurance and, of course, once the unemployment insurance runs out, that they can turn to welfare. My Party advocates strengthening the other programs that we have such as support programs for the family, namely universal family allowance and the child tax credit, so that families have the economic means to care for children. Children are expensive, and family allowance has obviously not kept up with the cost. The child tax credit is an important reform and we would like to see it raised and paid on a regular basis so that families would have the economic supports that they need. Of course, these economic supports are part of the entire functioning of a family, and when these supports are lacking, there is stress in the family which can result in family breakdown.
A proposal which I would like to stress as being an important support to the family would be the shorter work week for parents of young children. I think it would be desirable for
Marriage Breakdown
both parents to have the option of working shorter hours so that they could care for their young children themselves. My Party, of course, supports daycare programs. We think these programs are very important and often provide a very rich experience for children. These programs can be defended not only as a way of looking after children but as a way of providing education and cultural enrichment to children at a very young age. I would also like to stress that for many parents the preferable option is to look after their children themselves. If there were a shorter work week as a matter of right for parents of young children, that option could be exercised.
Of course, the state has an obligation to provide counselling services and crisis services in times of family breakdown to see if there can be a reconciliation. There is the possibility of teaching parenting skills that can improve the functioning of families.
As we are discussing marriage breakdown, Mr. Speaker, I would like to point out that it is important to understand that much of the burden of running a family and looking after the children is still borne by Canada's wives and mothers. Women put in a longer work week when both the paid work in the workforce and the unpaid work in the home are calculated. This, of course, puts an enormous strain on working mothers. Many mothers do need to work, and staying at home is not an option which is open to them. Women are putting in very, very long hours carrying the double burden of paid and unpaid work.
There are no adequate child care support services or daycare centres, and I must say as well that so far, Canadian husbands are still not performing their share of the unpaid work at home. I think that this matter must be raised as being one of the stresses that occurs in the family situation. In too many families, the father is a very distant disciplinarian in time of crisis and the provider of treats. He is not present nearly as often as the mother.
It has often been said that men need to be liberated from their sex roles as much as women do and that men have been too unexpressive, distant and that they have been part of the workforce and not part of the family unit. I expect that many men, if they were more closely involved with their children and did put in those hours of child care, would not only be relieving their wives of much of this heavy burden but would find as well that it is a very pleasurable experience. They would know their children better, their children would know them better and it would be a good experience both for the children and the father.
Rigid sex-role stereotyping harms men as much as it harms women and children. It is not simply a question of money and who pays for things, but a question of how people live, learn and use all of their talents. We would certainly like to see more child care talents developed in Canadian men.
There are a number of practical things that can be done by the state in times of crisis or family breakdown. We have seen indications that the state is beginning to provide various kinds

April 10, 1984
Marriage Breakdown
of counselling services, particularly in the realm of conflict resolution. Part of the problem of sexual stereotyping is that men are not supposed to be expressive but are supposed to be strong, silent types. When conflicts arise, they do not know how to express themselves in any other way than through violence. Thus there is the unhappy and shocking statistic that one in 10 Canadian wives is beaten by her husband in any given year. The experts tell us that one way of addressing this problem is to help people learn how to express their difficulties and conflicts in non-violent ways. We could promote programs which teach conflict resolution through negotiation and compromise without resorting to violence.
One proposal for dealing with the increasing rate of marriage breakdown is to make marriage itself more difficult to enter into. This is one of the proposals made by the Catholic bishops in their opposition to the divorce Bill which is before us. It is not our business to deal with the requirements for marriage as those fall under provincial jurisdiction. We can note, however, that it is very easy to be married very quickly, and we can only wish that it were otherwise.
I think one thing that the Standing Committee on Health, Welfare and Social Affairs could do would be to look into the situation of marriage counselling before marriage. Some churches are making it obligatory for couples to take marriage counselling before they are married in the church. There are plenty of examples of such counselling, and studies could be done to see if required marriage counselling before marriage has any beneficial effect. We could see if this makes for lasting marriages and prevents marriage breakdown. If so, the provincial governments, which are more directly involved in this, would have some idea of what to do. Perhaps they would then require marital counselling before marriage. That would certainly be something to consider if compulsory marriage counselling had very good results. If it did not, we could try other things.
I have heard very good things about marriage counselling programs. Obviously, anecdotal evidence is not sufficient. Simply an opinion here and there does not count. These programs should be properly and comprehensively studied. That is something which could be commissioned by a committee and something which our own National Health and Welfare Department could do.
I do not know that a comprehensive study in the sense of gathering more statistical information on marital breakdown needs to be done. I think we know that the statistics are very troubling. I do not think we need to have the statistics recited at any great length. However, I think we should be looking at the innovative programs which are being tried to improve the situation. We could encourage evaluation studies to see which of these programs are successful and which are not. We could promote further innovation and we could ensure that there is adequate evaluation so that we know where we stand. I have already mentioned that happening in the case of marriage counselling before marriage. It would be something to consider for conflict resolution projects which support the resolution of conflict without violence and with negotiation. There are a
great many parenting skills programs around the country. Let us evaluate them and see if they help keep families together. That is certainly a very proper function for a federal Department to perform.
Further, I think that we as a Parliament need to be addressing measures to combine family and work responsibilities so that people can participate in both. We live in a certain time and we are not going to go back to a time in which women will not want to work. I think those times are past us. We are going to need adequate measures to combine family and work responsibilities in a reasonable way so that there will not be excessive stresses on the family. We know what the problem is. We need policies to address the problem in a way that suits the times in which we live.
It is primarily the children who suffer as a result of family breakdown. Some experts have spoken about the right of children to stability and to have the marriage of their parents last so that their childhood home will last. It is very difficult to talk in those terms because even if we acknowledge at an abstract level that that right exists, how can we ensure that it exists in reality? Clearly, we can never guarantee such a right. It is a moral concept and perhaps a very good guiding concept, but it is not one we can immediately realize. It seems to me that, rather than talking in those abstract terms, what we should be doing is addressing the economic context, the stresses which are put on the family as a result of unemployment. We should begin to improve the practical and support measures for the family, which we have begun to provide in our society, the safety net we already have partially in place. These are the kinds of contributions we can make as parliamentarians to the support of the most important institution, the family.

speakeroldname: Mr. Ralph Ferguson (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: SOCIAL AFFAIRS
subsubtopic: ADVISABILITY OF EXAMINING MEASURES TO PREVENT MARRIAGE BREAKDOWN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to have the opportunity of addressing the House today on the motion of the Hon. Member for York-Sunbury (Mr. Howie) to have the problem of marriage breakdown referred to the Standing Committee on Health, Welfare and Social Affairs. The Hon. Member proposes to study the institution of the family in Canadian society and the role of government in assisting families. He is expressing the view that the institution of the family is in trouble in Canadian society and that we have to find ways of preventing these problems.
Let me first say that I fully share the Hon. Member's interest in the effects of marriage breakdown on family life and on the children in our society. I would like to take this opportunity, however, to express my views on the continuing strength and importance of family life and the ways in which government programs assist the family. We are all aware that Canadian families are changing. I do not believe, however,
I that this is a completely negative phenomenon. The changes we see in Canadian families should not be interpreted as signalling the demise of the institution of the family in Canada. It is more the case that change is simply giving birth
April 10, 1984

to new types of families and family units. The changes in Canadian families are due to many things, of which marital breakdown or divorce is only one element. There are also other factors, such as the postponement of the decision to have children by couples until their late twenties or thirties and the increasing participation of women in the labour force. All these factors are changing the patterns and demands of family life.
The importance of families to Canadians, however, continues to be very strong, as I can illustrate through some basic demographic data from the most recent census. The 1981 census tells us that over 80 per cent of the Canadian population continues to live in a family unit. In actual numbers there were over 6.3 million family units, out of over 8 million private households. Such figures lead me to think that the concept of the family is as strong today in Canadian society as it has ever been. Of course, the composition of these family units is not the same as it has been in the past. In the past we have always thought of the family as being composed of a husband, a wife and dependent children. Today, only one-half of the family units, roughly 3.5 million families, are these traditional families.
The definition of a family is now also normally thought of as including childless couples and single parents with children. The increase in the number of childless couples reflects the personal choices many couples now have in family planning. Couples may be career oriented and may wish to avoid or postpone childbirth for this reason. Many are also elderly couples whose children have grown and left home. With respect to single parent families, the changes have also been equally dramatic. The larger number of single parent families is due to marital separation or divorce. However, others are also formed through widowhood or as a result of births to unmarried mothers. We know that over 80 per cent of these single parent families are led by women.
I would also like to devote some attention to the topic of the "reconstituted" family. The reconstituted family results when previously divorced persons remarry and form new family units. It reflects the fact that as many as 75 per cent of divorced people remarry. This statistic in itself suggests that marriage remains popular even with those who have had a negative experience in a previous marriage. The reconstituted family effectively re-combines broken families into new units. They may bring together the children of one parent with new brothers and sisters from the new marriage. They obviously make a statement about the validity of marriage and family life, which we should not ignore. They also are likely to face a whole new set of problems with respect to child-rearing and responsibilities and adjustment of family members.
All these family types are different from the traditional nuclear family. But they are important in that they indicate that the institution of family remains very strong in Canadian society. The family unit, whether one has a single parent or remarried parents, remains very much the center and source of social, economic, and all other support for its members. Furthermore, I think we should fully expect that this diversity in
Marriage Breakdown
family patterns will continue. Lifestyles and attitudes are continually undergoing change in our society, and I believe families will adapt to these new challenges.
It is true that some of today's families are more likely to have special circumstances or problems. The single parent family, for example, is very likely to be headed by a woman who may lack job skills sufficient to support her family for extended periods of time. Similarly, even when there are two parents in the family, it is now more likely that the mother may work, so that outside child care arrangements have to be made. Today's families are more flexible than we would have expected of a family unit twenty years ago. And, due to these circumstances, they have special needs and demands for government services.
I would like to turn now to how the government has in fact provided many of these needed services and programs. I think the government has been very responsive and has shown its awareness and concern for families and changing situations in many ways. To illustrate, I can draw on a number of government programs which show support and commitment to the family. The basis of federal support to families has existed since the mid 1940's. I am referring here to the family allowance program which provides monthly benefits to families with dependent children up to age 18.
Family allowances are a universal program which provides a regular monthly payment of $29.95 per child to all families maintaining and caring for children, regardless of the income or employment status of the parents. In 1984, it provides an annual benefit of $359 per child. The allowances are a taxable benefit, and are taxed according to our progressive personal income tax system. After taxes, they provide highest benefits to low-income families and lowest benefits to high income families. Some 3.5 million families receive these benefits on behalf of their children at a cost of $2.4 billion dollars each year.
Since 1979, the federal Government has also provided the child tax credit which delivers additional assistance to low and middle income families to help them meet the costs of raising children. The child tax credit is income-tested on the basis of family income. In addition, it is a refundable credit, and so either reduces the taxpayer's tax liability or, in cases where the family's income is too low to have any tax liability, it provides a direct cash payment. For the 1983 tax year, a benefit of up to $343 dollars per child is available to families with incomes that are less than $26,330.
In essence, these two programs are the cornerstones of the federal government's direct support for families. Taken together, the family allowance and child tax credit programs currently provide maximum annual cash benefits of over $700 per child to eligible low income families which dependent children. This is a substantial benefit and clearly shows the Government's commitment to the principle of the family in Canada. The family allowance and child tax credit are normally delivered directly to mothers, and in this way are particularly beneficial to single parent, low-income families. Other programs such as the child tax exemption in the tax system,

April 10, 1984
Marriage Breakdown
and a deduction for child care expenses, are also designed to provide financial assistance to families.
Ever since the personal income tax system was introduced in 1917 some adjustment to the tax base has been allowed for the presence of dependent children. The exemption is currently $710 for a child under 18. Since this exemption provides higher benefits to those with highest incomes and no benefits to those with no taxable income, its value was de-indexed beginning in the 1984 tax year. Thus it will remain at $710 per child in the future.
The freezing of this exemption was one of a number of changes to the child benefits system which have been made over the last few years in order to improve the targeting of the child benefits system to families with low and moderate incomes.
Many women now participate in the paid labour force while maintaining their responsibilities for family and children at home. Women represent over 40 per cent of the workforce and their participation rates continue to rise. The existence of two earners is seen to be quite normal and important in today's families. Further, the result of this situation in which more women work outside the home is being felt in growing demands for related services such as child care and maternity benefits.
To assist working parents, the Income Tax Act allows a deduction for child care expenses for children under age 15. This deduction was first introduced in 1972, at a value of $500. Since then, however, progressive changes in the value and eligibility criteria for this deduction have taken place. These changes respond directly to the changing family structures and thus to the changing needs of families. Until 1983, the deduction had to be claimed by the working mother, except in special circumstances such as those in which the couple was legally separated, divorced, or the mother was infirm. In the 1983 Budget, the eligibility requirements were changed so that the lower income spouse is now required to claim the deduction, except under special circumstances. In this way, the deduction no longer discriminates between men and women. At the same time, the maximum value of the deduction was increased to $2,000 per child or two-thirds of earned income.
These changes respond to the increasing cost and use of child care. They ease the burden of child care expenses for families in which both parents work. In addition, the deduction is often particularly important for single parents who must work and support children.
I believe these changes demonstrate very well how government programs have recognized and accommodated the changing needs of families in Canada, both socially and economically. These programs are only part, however, of the network of programs which the Government effectively provides in response to the needs of Canadian families.
I would like to note a couple of other programs such as maternity benefits under the Unemployment Insurance Program and CEIC's Training Allowance Program both of which assist women and family in the labour force.
The Unemployment Insurance Act provides 15 weeks of paid maternity leave to eligible women who take time off work around the time of child birth. After a two-week waiting period, this program provides a paid benefit of 60 per cent of weekly insurable earnings, up to the maximum insurable earnings. In 1984, the maximum insurable earnings are set at $425, so UI maternity benefits will provide up to $255 per week for up to 15 weeks. Last year, there were about 121,000 allowable claims for UI maternity benefits at a cost of about $345 million.
As the Members of this Elouse will recall, there were also certain changes in the Unemployment Insurance Act, which were passed last year and which came into effect at the beginning of 1984. These changes were designed to make it easier for mothers to take advantage of UI maternity benefits.
For example, the legislative changes eliminated the "magic 10" rule. This rule required that a woman must have worked at least 10 weeks around the time of conception. It was judged to be unfair to some women who may have had a long work history but could not satisfy the 10 week rule. Also, a change was made allowing maternity benefits to be paid at any time in the initial benefit period. Previously, maternity benefits had to be claimed only during the first 15 weeks of a claim period. This change eliminated an inconsistency in the treatment of sickness and maternity benefits and made the provision of benefits more flexible. The new legislation also removed Section 46, which prevented women, who did not qualify for maternity benfits, from drawing regular UI benefits around the time of birth. Taken together, these changes significantly enhance the income protection provided to mothers by UI maternity benefits around the time of childbirth. In addition, changes were made to extend benefits to adopting parents. Under the new legislation, benefits are payable to either a father or a mother who takes time off work to meet responsibilities after the adoption of a child.
Finally, I would like to comment on how the National Training Act affects women and provides for their participation in the labour market. Under the National Training Program women are encouraged to train for non-traditional occupations, as well as other institutional and industrial training courses. Under the program, women who cannot get unemployment insurance benefits while on training, receive a training allowance for personal and dependant care expenses. The dependant care allowance is of considerable benefit to those women who are the sole supporters of their families, such as single parents who need financial help for child care while they are undertaking training. The rates paid under the Training Allowance Program were also increased last September. Again, this program demonstrates the flexibility and commitment of government programs in meeting the needs of women and families in the labour market.
In conclusion I would like to say that I believe the Government has demonstrated its awareness of the changing problems of families in Canada and provides a full network of programs

April 10, 1984

which are responsive to the social and economic needs of families. I know that the institution of the family is still strong in Canada, and I am sure that through its normal daily activities and programs the Government will continue to show its commitment and concern for the basic family structure in Canada.

subtopic: SOCIAL AFFAIRS
subsubtopic: ADVISABILITY OF EXAMINING MEASURES TO PREVENT MARRIAGE BREAKDOWN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to begin by complimenting the Member for York-Sunbury (Mr. Howie) for bringing this topic to the floor of the Chamber. Members may recall that the Member for York-Sunbury previously brought to the attention of this Chamber, through the Private Member's route, the issue of spousal battering. That motion received endorsation from this Chamber and subsequently went to the Standing Committee on Health and Welfare and Social Affairs. It resulted in a report, which is having impact on Canadian society and which is making the world a better place. Surely, Mr. Speaker, that exemplifies the highest traditions of this Chamber. It exemplifies what this Chamber should be all about.
I am curious about what we are going to find out 10 or 12 minutes from now. I am wondering whether the Liberal Government is willing to let this reference go to the Health and Welfare and Social Affairs Committee, or whether some member of the Liberal Party of Canada is going to stand up and speak through the hour of adjournment at six o'clock, thus effectively denying other Members of this Chamber the opportunity to examine the institution of the family and its place in Canadian society. Are they going to stop us from exercising what is in the minds of Canadians when they vote for us to come to this Chamber? They would like to know that the Parliament of Canada examines situations which should be examined. I think it is time for a committee of Parliament to begin to look at the family and to draw some conclusions about whether it is in good or bad shape, whether it has changed dramatically, and what we need to do to strengthen the atmosphere in which children can grow, develop and prosper.
It was after World War II that an agency of the Government, the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, provided a great amount of money to Canadians to get mortgages to build homes. At that particular time that Crown corporation decided that much of that mortgage money should go to homes which met certain criteria. One of the criterion they decided was important to Canadian homes of the future was the provision of a dining room. The architectural consequence of that, Mr. Speaker, was small kitchens. It took what had been a large facility in the home and divided it into two spaces; one called the dining room and the other called the kitchen.
Standing in this Chamber close to 40 years later I recognize that we have a great deal more marriage breakdown in Canada than we had some 40 years ago. I ask myself, as a social scientist, whether that policy decision by Central Mortgage and Housing is at least in part responsible for the breakdown of the family. I can certainly remember my own childhood. The kitchen was a large room and all the kids were around the kitchen table doing homework in the evening. Mom and Dad were there, perhaps reading a book, perhaps listening
Marriage Breakdown
to the radio. We did not have television in those days. The family was together. When it was cold outside, the family members were interacting together, getting to know each other and being supportive of each other.
An agency of the Government essentially decreed that this type of facility will not exist in Canadian homes in the future. This is done through lending policies and mortgage policies.
In speaking to this motion, I recall some questions that I have asked the Government in the past. I pointed out to Members of the House that if any one of them chose to get a divorce today and sign an agreement giving half of their income in support payments to their spouse, while continuing to live common law with that some spouse, they could save in excess of $2,000 in federal income tax. Is that a public policy direction that the Government has deliberately chosen? In economic terms it is a public policy which allows anyone who goes through the court procedure to have a formal marriage breakdown so as to have the tax system give them $200 a month in disposable income.
The former Minister of Finance, who is a bachelor, stood in the Chamber and told us in his Budget that every adult Canadian would be entitled to a piece of property that would be free of capital gains tax upon disposal except if he or she is married. That entitlement would be one-half on such a piece of property for married adult Canadians. This policy was formulated in the life of this Parliament. Is that a conscious public policy choice that was made by Cabinet Ministers and Members opposite? Are we getting signals from the Government that the traditional family shall be penalized in tax law and that the new forms of family structure will benefit from tax law?
I believe I am old enough to remember when a great many of my friends were in living arrangements that included grandparents, their children and grandchildren within the home. That does not happen very often any longer. Rather, public policy makes it economically better for all concerned to have the various parts of that extended family living in different places. The money that is available to Government is used to encourage a situation where senior citizens do not live with their children and grandchildren any longer. Is that a deliberate public policy choice by the Government? Is it a good choice?
The clearest demonstration of a fact that has bothered me during the life of this Parliament is that for over four years any significant Act affecting families that has been discussed in this Parliament has been under the responsibility of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde) and has been discussed by the Standing Committee on Finance along with other tax matters such as customs, excise tax and income tax. We have turned the Finance Committee of this Chamber into the primary screening body for social policy, particularly as that policy affects families. I suggest we have done a disservice to Canadian society and to families by doing that.

April 10, 1984
Marriage Breakdown
Earlier today, the only government Member to speak on this motion for referral of the issue of families to the standing comittee was the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Ferguson). It was a Finance Minister's speech. It did not deal with the heart of the issue, which is, in the first instance, a definition of what constitutes a family. What is a family in Canadian society and how does public policy impact on that family? Are we, as legislators, responsible for the change in family patterns that we are experiencing as a result of our taxation and other policies? Are we doing an adequate job in meeting the needs of the people living in those different family patterns?
I defy any Member in this Chamber to stand up and indicate that he has enough knowledge and has had enough time to examine those issues in order to reach conclusions. We can reach conclusions based on our own biases and ideologies, but I suggest that the issue is more complex. We could all benefit by knowing more about this issue. If the eight members of the Government sitting on the opposite side were simply to stay seated for the next three minutes, the subject matter of the Canadian family could go to the Committee on Health, Welfare and Social Affairs. That committee could work hard to study the issue of the Canadian family and decide whether something needs to be done. It may conclude that little or nothing should be done, or it may decide that much needs to be done. One Member, by standing in the House in the next two minutes, can decide for the whole country that the issue is not worth studying. I hope that no Member will do that, because a study of this issue is long overdue. The Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss Begin) is sitting in the front row. A signal from her to her colleagues to remain seated will allow the House to discuss the issue of the family and the impact of public policy on it. I hope Hon. Members will stay in their place and allow that to happen.

subtopic: SPACE WEAPONRY-ANTI-SATELLITE WEAPONS-CANADIAN POSITION. (B) REQUEST THAT CANADA REFUSE TO TEST ANTI-SATELLITE WEAPONS
SPACE WEAPONRY-ANTI-SATELLITE WEAPONS-CANADIAN POSITION. (B) REQUEST THAT CANADA REFUSE TO TEST ANTI-SATELLITE WEAPONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on Tuesday, April 3,1 asked the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) to press for a ban on anti-satellite and other space weapons. 1 also asked that Canada not participate in any way in the testing or development of anti-satellite or other "Star Wars" weapons or technologies. The Prime Minister did not answer my question. He said he would tell me some time about the Government's distinction between high and low altitude anti-satellite weapons. He did not address my question about anti-satellite weapons in general and space weapons in general. Not only was the Prime Minister's answer insufficient, it was also misleading.
At the present time neither the United States nor the Soviet Union possesses the capacity to pose a significant threat to the other's satellites. But developments are taking place for the first steps in this new-generation leap in the arms race and nuclear war fighting abilities. The Soviet Union has conducted 20 tests for anti-satellite weapons. Eleven of those tests have failed. Furthermore, the A-Sat is launched on an SS9 sized ICBM which has limited mobility and easy verification. In short, at the present state of development there is not yet a Soviet threat to deterrence or arms control.
The United States is now, this year, preparing to test its new generation anti-satellite known as the Prototype Miniature Air Launched System, PMALS. This small rocket will be launched from a high flying F-15 fighter aicraft. The Arms
April 10, 1984

Control Association in Washington, D.C. says this new weapon:
-will constitute a significant improvement over the existing Soviet A-Sat.
Writing for the Association, John Pike of the Federation of American Scientists also says:
Because of its small size, the PMALS will pose potentially insurmountable verification problems.
As we know, Mr. Speaker, the ability to verify the nature, number and location of weapons is the basis for any hope of nuclear arms control and limitation.
Ineffective Soviet tests have taken place. The United States, only this week encouraged by President Reagan's report to Congress, is proceeding with the tests of its own anti-satellite weapons, this new generation of weapons. Deployment and the threat of use have not yet taken place, but the time to act, the window of opportunity, is now.
That is why the Prime Minister is so misleading in calling for an artificial differentiation between high and low altitude anti-satellite weapons. All anti-satellite weapons should be banned, and they should be banned now before there are any such weapons deployed at any altitude.
Grave problems would arise if Canada were to work toward and help achieve a ban on only one level, or altitude, of anti-satellite weapons. The two superpowers would be permitted, indeed encouraged, to proceed with the development and deployment of a new generation of weapons for nuclear war fighting in space at some supposed "low" altitude already conceded by the Prime Minister. The technological developments that we do not want for any purpose would take place. Testing would take place. Deployment would take place, and it would be difficult, if not impossible, to assess and verify the flexibility and potential purpose of such weapons. Who could guarantee that weapons allowed for "low" altitude would not be used for "high" altitude? Who could control how the technology could be used once developed?
In his division of the universe into high and low altitudes, how would the Prime Minister address the problem of the majority of Soviet satellites that are presently in eliptical orbits around the earth which bring them into very close proximity to earth as well as the farther reaches of space?
It is understandable that the Prime Minister was advised in preparing his peace initiative proposals to draw this false distinction, hoping to appease Washington and gain the ear of the White House for his peace initiative. He chose not to take on the Reagan fast-action plans for these weapons, and chose instead to propose a ban on something further down the road, so-called "high altitude" anti-satellite weapons. This might have been a useful negotiating tactic to interest the Americans in his own proposals for arms control and better East-West relations. However, as the Prime Minister knows, the Reagan Administration did not accept his peace initiative proposals. And the Prime Minister knows that what might have been an acceptable negotiating position for his peace initiative should not be the Canadian Government policy on the general question of anti-satellite weapons and the militarization of space,
Adjournment Debate
at any altitude. There should be a ban on these weapons and a treaty to create such a ban.
The Soviet Union has placed before the United Nations what Canadian experts in arms control describe as "a perfectly acceptable treaty" to ban such weapons. The Soviet Union has offered to destroy its anti-satellite developments to date. Canada should pressure the United States to respond in a positive and constructive way to this opening proposal.
The Union of Concerned Scientists in the United States has reported that verification of such a treaty is possible. Only the Reagan administration is dismissing the possibility of verification and a treaty. The Reagan administration is precluding negotiations before they can begin, instead of negotiating to come to a verification agreement.
The Prime Minister should commit Canada to promoting a complete ban on anti-satellite and space-based weapons. The Prime Minister should certainly make it clear that Canada will not agree to take part in any way in the development and testing of such anti-satellite and space weapons. Finally, he should cease making this artificial differentiation between low and high altitudes.

speakeroldname: Mr. John Evans (Parliamentary Secretary to President of the Privy Council):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council
subtopic: SPACE WEAPONRY-ANTI-SATELLITE WEAPONS-CANADIAN POSITION. (B) REQUEST THAT CANADA REFUSE TO TEST ANTI-SATELLITE WEAPONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, during the Second United Nations Special Session on Disarmament in 1982, the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) drew attention to the urgency of coming to grips with the development of new weaponry for use in outer space. He noted how quickly in today's world science fiction had become reality and how inadequate the Treaty on Principles Governing the Activities of States in the Exploration and Use of Outer Space had become. There were loopholes in the Treaty which risked being highly destabilizing. He had in mind particularly anti-satellite weapons or anti-missile laser systems. As he pointed out then, "we cannot wait much longer if we are to be successful in foreclosing the prospect of space wars". He therefore proposed that an early start be made on a treaty to prohibit the development, testing and deployment of all weapons for use in outer space.
In the Committee on Disarmament in Geneva, now called the Conference on Disarmament, we have been working for the establishment of a working group to discuss outer space issues, including an anti-satellite treaty. We were close to reaching an agreement on setting up such a body at the 1983 session of the Conference on Disarmament, but the Soviet Union required time to refer the matter to Moscow. So far during the current session of the CD no agreement has been reached on this working group.
It is not surprising, in light of what I have already said, that in developing his initiative the Prime Minister focused on the question of outer space, and particularly anti-satellite weapons. We were aware that for some years the Soviet Union had been testing an anti-satellite system directed at low-flying satellites. By the beginning of this year the U.S.A. had also tested a comparable system. Neither superpower, however, has

April 10, 1984
Adjournment Debate
yet developed an anti-satellite system for high altitudes. It was our belief that an agreement not to do so was therefore still possible.
As part of his initiative, the Prime Minister proposed a ban on the testing and deployment of those anti-satellite systems designed to operate at high altitudes where the race has not yet begun. It was our view that such systems, by attacking global communications satellites which are located in high altitudes and which are of critical importance for crisis management, could be particularly destabilizing. It would leave an adversary blind and mute at the very moment when stability demands awareness and response. We are continuing our consultations with our NATO allies on this proposal.
Outer space is a subject to which we have been devoted and are continuing to devote a great deal of attention. Our whole approach to this question is governed by our concern about the possible militarization of outer space and its destabilizing effect on superpower relationships.

subtopic: CROWN CORPORATIONS-CONFLICT OF INTEREST INQUIRY
CROWN CORPORATIONS-CONFLICT OF INTEREST INQUIRY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to take part in the Adjournment Debate this evening as a result of a question I directed to the Minister of Transport (Mr. Axworthy) on March 28 following a planted question by a member on the Government side. I asked him what intentions he may have with respect to the disposition of the Northern Transportation Company. To my surprise the Minister replied that the Government was to privatize this Crown corporation.
Also I asked at that time whether there was any reason for me to suspect that this undue haste in the privatization of the Northern Transportation Company came about as a result of an inquiry started by the United States air force over the use of a piece of United States military equipment by the Northern Transportation Company, this Crown corporation. The answer the Minister gave me was that that was not true, that the reason the Government chose at this time to privatize Northern Transportation Corporation was based upon a change of economic circumstances.
I draw to the attention of the House the December 31, 1982 Consolidated Statement and Financial Position of NTCL. The current assets were $26,269,000, current liabilities of $9,860,000, leaving retained earnings assets in the company of some $16 million. Therefore, the Minister's explanation that it was based on a change of economic circumstances is suspect.
On January 10, 1984, the chairman of Northern Transportation Company Limited, Mr. Montpetit, met with representatives of the United States Air Force and the United States Government to discuss the use of the ARD-31. In questioning Mr. Montpetit, there was no mention to the United States Air Force at that time that there would be any privatization of the Northern Transportation Company. That was on January 10.
On February 21 Mr. Montpetit and Mr. Cameron were before the Standing Committee on Transport. They were
questioned as to the use of the ARD-31 and the relationship of that Crown corporation to the United States Air Force and, indeed, the Government of the United States on the use of United States military equipment. At that time Mr. Montpetit explained that over the past number of years they had made money using the ARD-31, but he did not explain it very fully. He said that in three years they lost money. We asked how the company managed to be on the profit side in Five years. He replied that in the first two years they broke even, in the next two years they made money and in the last year they lost money. According to Mr. Montpetit, they lost money in the last three years.
That led us to delve a little deeper into the operation of the ARD-31 and the Northern Transportation Company. By charging rates of up to $40,000 a day, which is not unusual for the use of a floating drydock, and not being flexible in the changing of those rates, the year that Mr. Montpetit said they lost money happened to be a year when they had no business, when they were unrealistic in their charges. The companies they had serviced prior refused to bid on business for their ships. At the same time, one of those companies, Arctic Transportation Company, felt that this Crown corporation was so inflexible that it brought in its own floating drydock to service its ships.
Consider the dates of the February 21 meeting of the standing committee and the January 10 meeting with Mr. Montpetit and the United States Air Force. I find it strange that Mr. Montpetit said that the relationship between this corporation and the United States Air Force was most cordial. He was very defensive when I asked whether there were some negotiations taking place between Northern Transportation Company and the United States Air Force for the purchase of the ARD-31. He said they were negotiating to purchase it and he believed they were to purchase the vessel in the very near future. They were operating at that time as an ongoing company.
It is strange with all this good relationship and the forthrightness with which this Crown corporation treated the United States Government, that a letter was sent by Congresswoman Pat Schroeder to the Hon. Verne Orr, Secretary of the Air Force, Attention: Legislative Liaison (Major Wayne Christine), Pentagon, Washington, listing some 12 questions which the United States Air Force wanted answered regarding the operation of the ARD-31.
That brings us to February 21, 1984, at which time there was no indication from the Chairman of the Board and the Chief Executive Officer during an entire sitting of the Standing Committee on Transport that the business was going to be privatized. However, from February 21 to March 28, a rush occurred, after an inquiry by the United States Air Force. There was even a suggestion by the United States Air Force that it would like to have the Adjutant-General take a look at the operation of this vessel and the Canadian Crown corporation with which it has contracts.
April 10, 1984

At that time, the company began to proceed with undue haste. It was indicated that the company would be privatized and disposed of as quickly as possible. As a matter of fact, I would not be at all surprised if directions have been sent that it should be disposed of within a month and a half, within perhaps six weeks. My colleague, the Hon. Member for Wetaskiwin (Mr. Schellenberger), says that it is to be six weeks. The Minister has sent directions to the President of NTCL that he is to be ready to sell that company within six weeks.
There is now undue haste, Mr. Speaker. There should be a full public inquiry into the operation of the ARD-31 before that money which legally belongs to the people of Canada is transferred into private hands.

subtopic: PUBLIC SERVICE-REPORTED ACCEPTANCE OF DIRECTORSHIP BY FORMER PRIVY COUNCIL OFFICIAL. (B) CONFLICT OF INTEREST GUIDELINES
PUBLIC SERVICE-REPORTED ACCEPTANCE OF DIRECTORSHIP BY FORMER PRIVY COUNCIL OFFICIAL. (B) CONFLICT OF INTEREST GUIDELINES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on April 2, 1984 I questioned the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) with respect to the announcement that one Michael J. L. Kirby had accepted an appointment to the Board of Directors of National Sea Products Ltd. It was my contention, Mr. Speaker, that Mr. Kirby's acceptance of such an appointment would be a violation of the conflict of interest guidelines for persons appointed to the Public Service.
Let me say for the record, Mr. Speaker, that Mr. Kirby is now a member of the other place with a designation of "South Shore". My concern and complaint relates to his capacity as a former public official, indeed an officer of the Privy Council. It was in that capacity that I raised my question and indicated my concern.
The proof of and the justification for my intervention is in the fact that a few days later, on April 5, 1984, Mr. Kirby announced that he had withdrawn from the process by which he would have been appointed to the Board of Directors of National Sea Products. Indeed, I take it that both the Prime Minister and Mr. Kirby would be prepared to admit that there was a potential violation, if not an actual violation, of the guidelines respecting conflict of interest.
My concern, as I rise in the House today, is not so much with the attitude of Mr. Kirby or the Prime Minister, but with the comments of the newspaper which originally reported the proposed appointment of Mr. Kirby to the Board of Directors of National Sea Products, that is the Halifax Chronicle-Herald. On April 7, 1984, the editorial writer for that newspaper indicated that National Sea Products in its desire to find the best possible people to serve on its Board of Directors had selected Mr. Kirby, but his withdrawal and, in the words of the

April 10, 1984
Adjournment Debate
article, the activity of his "quick-draw detractors" was not in the public interest. I would like to tell the editorial writers of The Chronicle-Herald, and the people of Canada, that I totally disagree with that position.
There is one thing the public demand from those in public office, whether the office be appointive or elective; that is honesty. By "honesty" I do not mean fair dealing in all transactions, but the avoidance of any suspicion that persons are not being fair in dealing with the duties and responsibilities placed upon them. The very purpose of conflict of interest rules is to avoid both the actual improper activity that might be perpetrated by holders of public office and, more importantly, even the suspicion of bad conduct on their part.
There is no question, Mr. Speaker, that the violation, or potential violation, was clear under the existing guidelines. One of the provisions of the guidelines states that an office holder must not, within the relevant time period, accept appointment to the board of directors of a commercial corporation which has as a matter of course a special relationship with the department or agency with which he was last employed.
There is no question that Mr. Kirby had a special relationship with National Sea Products Limited. In fact, the very newspaper which raised this matter contains a detailed report on the signing of an agreement between the Government of Canada, the Province of Nova Scotia, National Sea Products Limited and other parties interested in the restructuring of the Atlantic fishery. Mr. Kirby had been appointed specifically by the Minister of State for Economic and Regional Development Mr. Johnston to head the negotiating committee for the federal Government, not in his previous public office as secretary to the cabinet for federal-provincial relations. According to the Montreal Gazette he held a position as Deputy Clerk of the Privy Council. In addition, he himself said he held the position of Deputy Minister of Fisheries. Here was a person who held various kinds of public offices, clearly an officer in the public domain charged with the responsibility for dealing not only with the restructuring of the Atlantic fishery but the direct dealings with National Sea Products Limited and other companies connected with the Atlantic fisheries. For that person to then offer his services directly to the same company, National Sea Products Limited, in its commercial activities, is a violation of the worst kind.
That is exactly the kind of activity the guidelines are designed to prevent. They are intended to prevent public servants from going into commercial activity in the private sector and utilizing, or appearing to utilize, or risking the possibility that they will utilize, the information that has come to them in their public capacity as officers of the Government of Canada.
If that were not enough, Mr. Speaker, the same person, as I said, holds a position in the Senate. The provisions of the Senate and House of Commons Act are even clearer than the guidelines that would apply to them as public servants. Section 22(1) of that Act says:
No person, who is a member of the Senate, shall directly or indirectly, knowingly or wilfully be a party to or be concerned in any contract under which the public money of Canada is to be paid.
The whole point of the exercise of restructuring the Atlantic fisheries was to provide public funds for the companies engaged in the Atlantic fisheries. National Sea Products Limited would be the beneficiary of millions of dollars of public funds. Mr. Kirby was ready to deal with them in his private capacity. I have said that honesty is the most important element expected of public officers, public servants and elected politicians. We must do everything we can to protect the public from any possible dishonesty or any indication of dishonesty.
Recently Bruce MacDonald was taken away from Revenue Canada as the Deputy Minister. How would you like it if he went to work for H and R Block and told the citizens of Canada that he was now prepared to prepare their tax returns knowing all he had learned in Revenue Canada? Mr. Speaker, the editorial comment is nonsense, not acceptable-

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in response to an allegation of conflict of interest raised by the Hon. Member for Halifax West (Mr. Crosby) on April 2, the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) agreed to take notice of the question and to seek the facts. I am glad to have this occasion to lay the facts of this case before Hon. Members of the House. I particularly appreciate having the opportunity to correct the misguided notions and misguided statements just made by the Hon. Member for Halifax West.
It is a fact, Mr. Speaker, that Michael Kirby is not on the Board of Directors of National Sea Products Limited and that he never was on that Board. As a consequence, there is absolutely no basis to the allegation that Mr. Kirby is in a conflict of interest situation. The allegation is hypothetical and conjectural and is not founded in fact. The Hon. Member is taking a partisan approach by attacking the reputation of a respected Canadian who is committed to the economic revitili-zation of the Atlantic fisheries. Mr. Kirby is a man of established abilities and experience who has worked very hard to help bring about the successful restructuring of the Atlantic fisheries.
It is a touch of irony, Mr. Speaker, that the very newspaper which raised the matter of Mr. Kirby's nomination should, in a subsequent editorial, praise Mr. Kirby. I would like to quote from The Halifax Chronicle Herald of April 7, 1984, from which my friend from Halifax West also quoted. It said:
It is a sad thing for the fisheries that he cannot answer-
Mr. Speaker, this is terribly important:
-positively a request by the company that he became a member of the Board, although it is a mark of his integrity that he considered the issue and withdrew.
The point is, Mr. Speaker, that he was offered a position on the Board by the company. The Hon. Member for Halifax West implied that Mr. Kirby offered his services to National
April 10, 1984

Sea Products. That is totally false. National Sea Products offered Mr. Kirby a place on the Board. Mr. Kirby considered and withdrew. He did the honourable thing. I wish I could say the same thing for the Hon. Member who raised the issue in the House.
